title: Data centres in India: capacity, cities, companies, policy and power (2026)
description: India had about 1.6 to 1.8 GW of live data centre capacity in mid-2026, half of it in Mumbai. How many data centres there are, where, who runs them, the rules that apply and how they get power.
intro: India had between 1.6 GW and 1.8 GW of operational data centre capacity in mid-2026, depending on who counts and what they count; the government told Parliament in August 2026 that capacity had grown from 375 MW in 2020 to about 1,575 MW. Mumbai holds about half of it. Cushman & Wakefield counted 147 data centres across the top seven cities in H1 2026, with 509 MW under construction and 3,351 MW more planned. Forecasts for 2030 run from about 5.6 GW to 8 GW. Crisil Ratings says the pace of the build-out will hinge on timely power connectivity, regulatory approvals and project execution.
takeaways: Live capacity (mid-2026): about 1.6 GW (JLL), 1,789 MW (Cushman & Wakefield, top seven cities), 1,819 MW (Savills), with CBRE expecting 2 GW by the end of 2026.
Mumbai has about 50% of operational capacity; Chennai 12%, Delhi NCR 10%, Bengaluru 9%, Hyderabad 8%, Pune 7%, Kolkata 2%.

There is still no notified national data centre policy. Data centres of 5 MW IT load or more have infrastructure status (2022), and Budget 2026-27 added a tax holiday to 2047 for foreign cloud firms using Indian data centre services.
The Central Electricity Authority estimates data centre power demand of about 17 GW by 2031-32.

sections.heading: How much data centre capacity does India have?

blocks.text: Five research houses published H1 2026 figures. They agree on the order of magnitude and disagree on the last few hundred MW, partly because they count different things: SBI counts only colocation, Cushman & Wakefield counts colocation and hyperscale cloud in the top seven cities but excludes captive facilities, and Savills includes enterprise and edge facilities.

blocks.text: Additions in H1 2026 ranged from 85 MW (JLL) to 178 MW (Cushman & Wakefield) and 258 MW of IT load (Savills). Hyperscalers took more than 80% of absorption in the half, and pre-leased capacity roughly doubled to 1.15 GW.

sections.heading: How big will India’s data centre market be by 2030?

blocks.text: Crisil expects about three quarters of the roughly 6 GW now upcoming to sit in Visakhapatnam, Mumbai and Hyderabad, and the hyperscaler share of leased capacity to rise from 60 to 65% in FY26 to 75 to 80% by FY30. It reports contract tenors have lengthened to 15 to 20 years.

sections.heading: Where are India’s data centres?

blocks.text: Mumbai has 13 cable landing stations, with two more due in 2026, and its Thane-Belapur Road cluster alone holds 675 MW in operation. Hyderabad has the second-largest share of upcoming supply. Cushman & Wakefield maps more than 4 GW of early-stage or announced capacity at Visakhapatnam and more than 1 GW at Jamnagar in Gujarat.

sections.heading: What policy applies to data centres in India?

blocks.text: There is no notified national data centre policy. MeitY issued a draft in November 2020 that was never notified, and revived consultations in August 2025. On 14 October 2026 NITI Aayog released a Data Centre Evaluation Framework, described as a guidance document, that asks each state to publish a data centre approval matrix and bring clearances onto one digital interface.

items: Infrastructure status: data centres of at least 5 MW IT load were added to the Harmonised Master List under Communication on 11 October 2022; Anarock says the status has improved access to long-tenor financing.

Tax: Budget 2026-27, enacted through the Finance Act 2026, exempts foreign cloud companies from tax from tax year 2026-27 to 2046-47 on income from serving global customers using Indian data centre services; a 15% cost safe harbour applies where the Indian provider is related.

States: as of September 2026, 11 states had dedicated data centre policies in force. Priority incentives include land concessions, stamp duty and electricity duty exemptions and single-window facilitation.

blocks.text: Demand is also driven by data rules: RBI requires payment system data to be stored only in India (2018); SEBI requires regulated entities’ cloud data to stay within India (2023); CERT-In requires 180 days of logs kept in India and five years of subscriber records from data centres (2022); and the DPDP Rules 2025, notified in November 2025 with an 18-month phased compliance timeline, require significant data fiduciaries to comply with government-specified restrictions on certain data, including localisation where required.

sections.heading: How do India’s data centres get power?

blocks.text: Data centre capacity is less than 1% of India’s installed power capacity, the government told Parliament, but the Central Electricity Authority puts data centre power demand at about 17 GW by 2031-32. Locally the numbers are already large: Crisil estimates that by FY2030 data centre capacity could equal about 60% of Mumbai’s current peak demand and about 80% of Visakhapatnam’s.

Structure Research reports that MSEDCL has allocated about 6 GW of grid capacity to data centres in Navi Mumbai and that committed and under-construction capacity is approaching that threshold, pushing new builds to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani, where separate substation infrastructure can be commissioned. For a site buyer, the document behind the MW and the date of the connection matter more than distance to a line.

sections.heading: What does a data centre cost in India?

blocks.text: Cushman & Wakefield benchmarks construction at US$7.4 million per MW, about 23% below Malaysia, and uses US$9.0 million per MW for incremental AI capacity. SBI’s sector report gives ₹50 to 55 crore per MW for an air-cooled Tier III, non-AI build and up to ₹75 crore for AI facilities with immersion cooling or Tier IV.

Wholesale colocation for 5 MW and above was quoted at ₹6,000 to 7,500 per kW per month in Mumbai in H1 2025, Cushman & Wakefield’s latest rent table (its H1 2026 report has none). Anarock puts land for 100 to 500 MW parks at ₹3 to 10 crore per acre and for small suburban Mumbai sites at ₹35 to 60 crore.

sections.heading: AI data centres and GPUs in India

blocks.text: Under the IndiaAI Mission, more than 38,000 GPUs had been onboarded and offered at ₹65 per hour by February 2026. Announced AI campuses include Google’s AI hub in Visakhapatnam, Reliance’s multi-gigawatt build at Jamnagar and TCS HyperVault, whose first customer is OpenAI. Anarock puts an Nvidia H100 GPU cluster at 30 to 60 kW per rack against 8 to 10 kW traditionally.

faqs.question: How many data centres are there in India?
faqs.answer: Cushman & Wakefield counted 147 operational data centres run by 33 operators across the top seven cities in H1 2026; Anarock counted 164 operational data centres. By capacity, India had about 1.6 to 1.8 GW live in mid-2026.

faqs.question: What is the total data centre capacity in India in 2026?
faqs.answer: About 1,575 MW according to the government (August 2026), 1,789 MW across the top seven cities according to Cushman & Wakefield (H1 2026) and 1,819 MW of IT load according to Savills. CBRE expects 2 GW by the end of 2026.

faqs.question: Which city has the most data centres in India?
faqs.answer: Mumbai, with 890 MW or about half of India’s operational capacity in H1 2026, most of it in Navi Mumbai along Thane-Belapur Road. Chennai is second with 214 MW.

faqs.question: Which state has the most data centres in India?
faqs.answer: Maharashtra: Mumbai (50%) and Pune (7%) together hold more than half of operational capacity on Cushman & Wakefield’s H1 2026 count, and Chennai in Tamil Nadu is next at 12%. For pipeline, Hyderabad has the second-largest share of upcoming supply (18%), and more than 4 GW of early-stage or announced capacity is mapped at Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh.

faqs.question: Does India have a national data centre policy?
faqs.answer: Not a notified one. MeitY’s 2020 draft was never notified and consultations were revived in August 2025. National measures in force include infrastructure status for data centres of 5 MW IT load or more (2022) and the Budget 2026-27 tax holiday for foreign cloud firms using Indian data centres, enacted through the Finance Act 2026.

faqs.question: How much electricity will Indian data centres need?
faqs.answer: The Central Electricity Authority estimates data centre power demand of about 17 GW by 2031-32. Current data centre capacity is less than 1% of India’s installed power capacity.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to build a data center in India per MW?
faqs.answer: About US$7.4 million per MW on Cushman & Wakefield’s benchmark, which excludes land, or ₹50 to 55 crore per MW for an air-cooled Tier III build and up to ₹75 crore for AI or Tier IV builds according to SBI’s sector report.

faqs.question: What are the largest data centre projects in India?
faqs.answer: Announced gigawatt-scale campuses include Google’s AI hub in Visakhapatnam (about US$15 billion over 2026 to 2030) and Reliance’s multi-gigawatt build at Jamnagar. Cushman & Wakefield maps more than 4 GW of early-stage or announced capacity in Visakhapatnam alone.

title: How to find a data centre site in India: power, fibre, land and risk (2026)
description: Pick an Indian data centre site in this order: written power evidence, fibre and cable landings, land and zoning, water, physical risk, then state policy. City by city comparison with sources.
intro: The best location for a data centre in India is the one that can show a dated power connection for the full load, not the one nearest a substation. Mumbai has half of India’s operational capacity and 13 cable landing stations, but the roughly 6 GW of grid capacity allocated to Navi Mumbai data centres is close to fully committed. Chennai and Hyderabad have spare colocation (vacancy of 26.7% and 28.0% in H1 2026), and Visakhapatnam has more than 4 GW announced. Screen power evidence first, then fibre, land and zoning, water, seismic and flood risk, and the state policy that applies.
takeaways: Rank sites by the document behind the MW (connection offer, sanctioned load, signed agreement), not by distance to a line.
Mumbai and Chennai have the cable landings; Hyderabad, Noida and Pune are inland markets that depend on terrestrial fibre.
Seismic zones in the IS 1893 (Part 1):2002 town list: Delhi IV; Mumbai, Chennai, Pune, Kolkata and Ahmedabad III; Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Visakhapatnam II.
Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy covered data centres incorporated until 31 March 2026 and Uttar Pradesh replaced its 2021 policy in July 2026, so check which incentives are open on the date you apply.

sections.heading: The order to screen a site in

blocks.text: Each check can kill a site, so run the cheapest decisive check first. In India that is power: a large load needs a dedicated connection from the discom or the state transmission utility, and the date on that connection usually sets the project schedule. NITI Aayog’s October 2026 framework now asks states to verify power and water capacity before clearing data centre projects.

sections.heading: Power: the check that decides the schedule

blocks.text: Structure Research reports that MSEDCL allocated about 6 GW of grid capacity to Navi Mumbai data centres and that committed and under-construction capacity is approaching it, which is pushing new builds to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani where new substations can be built. Crisil estimates that by FY2030 data centre capacity could equal about 60% of Mumbai’s current peak demand and about 80% of Visakhapatnam’s.

Some state policies write the connection terms down: Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy offered dual grid supply for a sanctioned load of 50 MW or more and an additional feeder above 100 MW, and West Bengal’s 2021 policy said the government would establish dual power grid networks. Treat these as eligibility for a connection, not as capacity on a given date.

sections.heading: Fibre and cable landings

blocks.text: Tele.net reports that the Mumbai region handles about 95% of India’s international bandwidth. Mumbai has 13 cable landing stations with two more due in 2026, and Chennai has 7 with two under construction. Visakhapatnam is being built as an east coast gateway: Google’s America-India Connect, announced on 18 February 2026, includes a subsea path from Visakhapatnam and Chennai to South Africa and one from Visakhapatnam to Singapore.

For an AI training campus, latency to a landing station matters less than power and land; for interconnection and cloud regions it matters more. Decide which you are building before weighting this step.

sections.heading: Land, water and physical risk

blocks.text: Anarock prices land for 100 to 500 MW parks at ₹3 to 10 crore per acre and for small suburban Mumbai sites at ₹35 to 60 crore, and advises buying 30 to 50% more land than phase 1 needs. Groundwater cannot be assumed: under the CGWA guidelines of September 2020, new industries other than MSMEs get no groundwater NOC in over-exploited assessment units, and SBI names Bengaluru, Chennai and Gurugram as water-stressed data centre metros.

Physical risk is mostly known in advance: 944 mm of rain fell on Mumbai on 26 July 2005, a 24-hour record for the city, Chennai’s Meenambakkam station recorded 1,178.3 mm in November 2015, and Cyclone Hudhud crossed the coast over Visakhapatnam in October 2014. AAI height clearance is needed within 20 km of an airport operating under visual flight rules and 56 km of one under instrument flight rules, and new airports began commercial flights at Navi Mumbai in December 2025 and at Noida in June 2026.

faqs.answer: It depends on what you are building. Mumbai has the cable landings and half of operational capacity but a tight grid in Navi Mumbai; Chennai has landings and 26.7% colocation vacancy; Hyderabad has the second-largest pipeline and seismic zone II; Visakhapatnam has more than 4 GW announced. faqs.question: Which Indian cities have cable landing stations for data centres?
faqs.answer: Mumbai (13 stations, two more due in 2026) and Chennai (7, two under construction) are the main ones. Google has announced a new international subsea gateway at Visakhapatnam, and a station at Tajpur near Kolkata is under construction.

faqs.answer: Structure Research reports that the roughly 6 GW of grid capacity MSEDCL allocated to Navi Mumbai data centres is close to fully committed, and that new builds are moving to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani where new substations can be built.

title: Approvals needed for a data centre in India: permits, NOCs and who issues them
description: A data centre in India needs land and building approvals, environmental clearance above 20,000 sq m, pollution board consents, groundwater, airport height and fire NOCs, a diesel licence and electrical inspection.
intro: There is no single data centre licence in India. A project collects approvals from several authorities: land allotment and building plan approval from the state or local authority, environmental clearance under the EIA Notification 2006 if the built-up area is 20,000 sq m or more, Consent to Establish and Consent to Operate from the state pollution control board, a groundwater NOC, an airport height clearance, a fire NOC, a licence to store diesel and an electrical inspector’s approval before energisation. NITI Aayog’s October 2026 framework asks every state to publish a data centre approval matrix and run a single clearance portal because these sit with so many offices.
takeaways: Environmental clearance: the environment ministry told the Rajya Sabha on 6 August 2026 that AI data centres do not per se need it, only as building projects above 20,000 sq m (item 8(a)) or townships (item 8(b)).

Pollution board category: CPCB’s January 2025 classification says data centres polluting only through gensets may be classified by genset capacity and fuel: 1 MVA or more on liquid fuel is Orange, on gas Green.
Diesel: for Class B petroleum (confirm your fuel’s class with PESO), below 2,500 litres needs no licence, 2,500 to 25,000 litres is licensed by the district authority and more needs a PESO licence.
Fire: the National Building Code 2016 puts electronic data processing centres in occupancy E-3 and requires automatic fire detection and alarm.

sections.heading: Does a data centre need environmental clearance in India?

blocks.text: Item 8(a) of the EIA Notification 2006 covers building and construction projects of 20,000 sq m or more and below 1,50,000 sq m of built-up area; item 8(b) covers townships and area development projects of 50 ha or more or 1,50,000 sq m or more. In a Rajya Sabha reply on 6 August 2026, the environment ministry said AI data centres do not per se require clearance but do when proposed as part of a project under 8(a) or 8(b), and that SEIAA grants clearance for such building projects.

SEIAA Maharashtra granted clearance under item 8(a) on 21 November 2025 for Nxtra’s expansion at Mahape, Navi Mumbai: two data centre buildings, two DG buildings and a substation building, 76,930 sq m built-up in total after expansion. STT GDC received an 8(a) clearance from SEIAA Maharashtra in April 2022. In August 2025 the Supreme Court struck down the part of a January 2025 notification that had exempted industrial sheds, schools, colleges and hostels from prior clearance under 8(a).

sections.heading: What are CTE and CTO, and which category is a data centre?

blocks.text: Consent to Establish (CTE) is the state pollution control board’s permission to build; Consent to Operate (CTO) is its permission to run. Both are issued under the Water Act 1974 and the Air Act 1981, and the conditions follow the sector’s category.

rows: Standalone gensets totalling less than 1,000 kVA
Gensets totalling 1 MVA or more on liquid fuel
Gensets totalling 1 MVA or more on cleaner or gaseous fuel
Building construction, built-up area of 20,000 sq m or more

blocks.text: CPCB notes that data centres whose pollution potential comes only from gensets may be classified by genset capacity and fuel, so a campus with diesel gensets of 1 MVA or more falls in Orange, for which boards may grant CTO for up to 10 years, against 15 years for Green. Confirm the category with the state board for the specific site.

sections.heading: Diesel storage and genset rules

blocks.text: The Petroleum Rules 2002 split fuels by flash point: Class B is 23°C to below 65°C. PESO lists diesel (HSD) among products that need a licence. Class B storage below 2,500 litres needs no PESO licence, the district authority licenses more than 2,500 and up to 25,000 litres, and larger quantities need a PESO licence; PESO’s FAQ says applicants register on the National Single Window System first. Confirm the class of the fuel you store with PESO; at data centre volumes it decides which licence you need.

CPCB told the National Green Tribunal that revised emission standards for genset engines up to 800 kW were notified by G.S.R. 804(E) of 3 November 2022 and are regulated at the manufacturing stage, while diesel engines above 800 kW fall under G.S.R. 489(E) of 9 July 2002 and are regulated by the state pollution control boards.

items.label: Diesel generators and backup power rules

sections.heading: Fire NOC and electrical inspection

blocks.text: The National Building Code 2016, Part 4, puts electronic data processing centres and computer installations in occupancy E-3. For E-3 it requires an automatic fire detection and alarm system, allows clean agents, mist technologies or hypoxic air for protection, and allows CO2 or inert gas flooding for electrical panels. Anarock lists the fire NOC as issued by the state fire department.

Under the CEA safety regulations of 2023, each state notifies the voltage up to which owners may self-certify. Andhra Pradesh’s order of 11 March 2026 sets 33 kV: installations above it are inspected by the electrical inspector, and generating units above 10 kW are inspected before commissioning. In Andhra Pradesh, then, a campus with a 66, 110 or 220 kV substation and diesel gensets needs the inspector before energisation.

sections.heading: Obligations that start once the data centre runs

items: CERT-In directions of 28 April 2022: report listed cyber incidents within 6 hours, keep ICT logs for 180 days in India, and keep validated subscriber records for 5 years.
Battery Waste Management Rules 2022: producers carry extended producer responsibility under the CPCB EPR system; confirm how waste UPS batteries must be handed over.
Energy codes: BEE has notified ECBC 2017 and ECSBC 2024, which include provisions relevant to data centre infrastructure.
Refrigerants: India’s HFC production and consumption freeze starts on 1 January 2028, with an 85% cut by 2047, which affects chiller refrigerant choice.

faqs.question: What approvals are needed to set up a data centre in India?
faqs.answer: Typically: land allotment or purchase and any change of land use, building plan approval, environmental clearance if built-up area is 20,000 sq m or more, Consent to Establish and Consent to Operate from the state pollution control board, a groundwater NOC, an AAI height clearance near airports, a diesel storage licence, a fire NOC and electrical inspection before energisation.

faqs.question: Is there a data center licence in India?
faqs.answer: No single licence. A data centre collects approvals from several authorities. NITI Aayog’s October 2026 framework asks each state to publish a data centre approval matrix and run a single clearance portal.

faqs.question: Does a data centre need environmental clearance?
faqs.answer: Not as a category. The environment ministry told the Rajya Sabha on 6 August 2026 that AI data centres do not per se require it, but do when proposed as a building project above 20,000 sq m (item 8(a) of the EIA Notification 2006) or a township of 50 ha or 1,50,000 sq m or more (item 8(b)).

faqs.question: What is CTE and CTO for a data centre?
faqs.answer: Consent to Establish and Consent to Operate are the state pollution control board’s permissions to build and to run, under the Water Act 1974 and the Air Act 1981. Under CPCB’s January 2025 classification a data centre polluting only through gensets may be classified by its gensets: 1 MVA or more on liquid fuel is Orange.

faqs.question: Which pollution category is a data centre in India?
faqs.answer: CPCB’s January 2025 classification says projects such as data centres whose pollution potential comes only from gensets may be classified by genset capacity and fuel: Orange for 1 MVA or more on liquid fuel, Green on cleaner or gaseous fuel. A building construction project of 20,000 sq m or more is separately Orange.

faqs.question: Do I need a licence to store diesel at a data centre?
faqs.answer: Under the Petroleum Rules 2002, Class B fuel below 2,500 litres needs no licence, 2,500 to 25,000 litres needs a district licence and more needs a PESO licence. PESO lists diesel (HSD) as a product requiring a licence; confirm its class for your fuel with PESO.

faqs.question: Do data centres need a fire NOC?
faqs.answer: Yes. Anarock lists the fire NOC as issued by the state fire department, and the National Building Code 2016 puts electronic data processing centres in occupancy E-3, which requires automatic fire detection and alarm.

title: How to set up a data centre in India: from entity to energisation (2026)
description: Setting up a data centre in India runs in nine steps: size the load, form the entity, pick a state, confirm power, secure land, design to Indian codes, get approvals, inspect and energise.
intro: To set up a data centre in India, fix the load and tier, form an Indian company (Khaitan & Co notes that 100% foreign investment is permitted under the automatic route for a company doing only data centre business), choose a state whose policy is actually open, and confirm a dated power connection before you buy land. Then secure the land, design to the National Building Code and IS 1893, collect the pre-construction approvals, build, pass fire and electrical inspection, and take Consent to Operate. Data centres of 5 MW IT load or more in a dedicated building have infrastructure status, which Anarock says has improved access to long-tenor financing. The order matters more than any single permit: a site without a dated power connection is not a site.
takeaways: Power before land: get the voltage, MW and date in writing for each candidate site.
Foreign investors: 100% under the automatic route according to Khaitan & Co, except investors from land-border countries, who need government approval under Press Note 3 (2020).
Data centres in a dedicated building with 5 MW of IT load or more are infrastructure (Harmonised Master List, 11 October 2022).
The detailed permit list, with authorities and thresholds, is on the approvals page.

sections.heading: The nine steps

rows: 1. Size the load and the tier

Fix the IT load in MW, the phasing, the target tier and the rack density. Anarock puts an Nvidia H100 GPU cluster at 30 to 60 kW per rack against 8 to 10 kW traditionally, which changes power, cooling and land.

Khaitan & Co notes that 100% foreign investment is permitted under the automatic route in an Indian company engaged only in the data centre business. Investors from countries that share a land border with India, or whose beneficial owner is in one, need government approval under Press Note 3 (2020).
3. Shortlist states and check which policies are open

Compare the state policies that are in force on the date you will apply. Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy covered data centres incorporated up to 31 March 2026; Uttar Pradesh replaced its 2021 policy in July 2026.
4. Confirm the power path before buying land

Get the serving discom or transmission utility, the voltage, the MW and the date in writing for each candidate site. In Navi Mumbai the grid capacity allocated to data centres is reported close to fully committed.
5. Secure land and run site due diligence
Take an allotment from a state development authority or buy private land, then check title, land use, flood and seismic exposure, groundwater status and airport height limits.

National Building Code 2016 Part 4 (occupancy E-3), IS 1893 (Part 1):2016 for seismic design, BEE’s ECBC 2017 or ECSBC 2024, and the BIS adoptions of ISO/IEC 22237 and 30134 where you want a recognised standard.
Building plan, environmental clearance if built-up area is 20,000 sq m or more, Consent to Establish, groundwater NOC, airport height clearance and the diesel storage licence.
8. Build, inspect and get the operating consents
Fire NOC, electrical inspector approval before energisation and Consent to Operate from the state pollution control board.
9. Energise, claim incentives and start operating compliance
Register for state incentives through the single window, and set up CERT-In reporting and log retention, battery and e-waste handling, and energy and water reporting.

items.label: Approvals for a data centre in India

sections.heading: Entity, foreign investment and finance

blocks.text: Khaitan & Co notes that 100% FDI is permitted under the automatic route in Indian companies engaged only in the data centre business, and that if the company also owns fibre assets, the conditions for that sector apply. Under Press Note 3 (2020), an entity of a country that shares a land border with India, or whose beneficial owner is situated in or is a citizen of such a country, can invest only under the government route; Bar & Bench notes that Press Note 2 (2026) kept that requirement.

Data centres housed in a dedicated building with at least 5 MW of IT load were added to the Harmonised Master List of Infrastructure on 11 October 2022. Anarock reports long-tenor debt for data centres at about 9.5 to 10.5% for up to 12 years, helped by that status.

sections.heading: Choosing the state

blocks.text: State policies decide capital subsidy, stamp duty, electricity duty and power terms. Two changed in 2026: Uttar Pradesh notified a new policy on 9 July 2026 that repeals the 2021 one, and Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy applied to data centres incorporated from 1 April 2021 to 31 March 2026. Read the notified text and its validity date, not a summary.

items.label: Infrastructure status, tax holiday and DC SEZs

sections.heading: Power and land, in that order

blocks.text: A large data centre needs a dedicated connection from the discom or the state transmission utility. Structure Research reports that the roughly 6 GW of grid capacity MSEDCL allocated to Navi Mumbai data centres is close to fully committed, which is why new campuses there are moving to sites where new substations can be built. NITI Aayog has asked states to verify power and water capacity before clearing projects.

Allotment from a state development authority usually comes with defined use and building norms. Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 policy, for example, gives data centres FAR 3.0 free plus 1.0 chargeable, ground coverage of up to 60% or as per byelaws, and a 100% stamp duty exemption on land bought or leased from a government authority.

sections.heading: Design standards to plan around

blocks.text: The National Building Code 2016 puts electronic data processing centres in occupancy E-3. For seismic design, BIS lists IS 1893 (Part 1):2016 among its published standards and the 2025 edition of Part 1 as withdrawn. BIS has adopted the ISO/IEC 22237 facility series and the ISO/IEC 30134 metrics (including PUE, WUE and CUE), and Business Standard reports that these standards are voluntary.
Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 policy offers a one-time reimbursement of 25% of Tier III and 50% of Tier IV certification charges by Uptime, TIA or an equivalent approved agency.

sections.heading: After energisation

blocks.text: Operating obligations start on day one: CERT-In’s 2022 directions require incident reports within 6 hours, 180 days of logs kept in India and 5 years of subscriber records from data centres; and producers carry extended producer responsibility for UPS batteries under the Battery Waste Management Rules 2022, so confirm the hand-over route for waste batteries.

blocks.text: Invariant works on the steps that decide whether a site is real: it checks how the site gets power and the evidence behind the MW, screens seismic, flood, groundwater and airport height risk, and maps the central and state approvals with the authority behind each one. Send the state, the MW and the date you need power.

title: Data centre cost per MW in India: ₹35 to 75 crore to build, plus land (2026)
description: Building a data centre in India costs about US$7.4 million per MW on Cushman & Wakefield’s benchmark, and ₹35 to 75 crore per MW on SBI’s figures depending on scale, tier and cooling. Benchmarks, land, rents and financing.
intro: Published benchmarks put the cost of building a data centre in India at ₹35 crore to ₹75 crore per MW of IT load: SBI’s April 2026 sector report gives ₹35 to 45 crore for large facilities, ₹50 to 55 crore for an air-cooled Tier III build and up to ₹75 crore for AI with immersion cooling or Tier IV. Cushman & Wakefield benchmarks US$7.4 million per MW, about 23% below Malaysia and 26% below Australia, and assumes US$9.0 million per MW for incremental AI capacity in its projections. Anarock prices land separately, at ₹3 crore to ₹60 crore per acre across its size bands, and reports long-tenor debt at about 9.5 to 10.5%.
takeaways: Cushman & Wakefield: US$7.4 million per MW; it assumes US$9.0 million per MW for incremental AI capacity.
SBI (April 2026): ₹50 to 55 crore per MW for air-cooled Tier III, up to ₹75 crore for AI with immersion cooling or Tier IV, ₹35 to 45 crore for large facilities.
Anarock: ₹40 to 45 crore per MW (low) to ₹65 to 70 crore per MW (high) for a greenfield Tier III N+1 build.
Wholesale colocation for 5 MW and above rented at about ₹6,000 to 7,500 per kW per month in H1 2025.

sections.heading: How much does it cost to build a data centre in India per MW?

₹40 to 45 crore per MW to ₹65 to 70 crore per MW (US$4.8 to 8.4 million)

blocks.text: Anarock prices land separately, per acre. Crisil puts Indian development costs about one fifth below several competing Asia Pacific markets.

A cross-check from the sector level: ICRA expected third-party capacity to grow from 1,250 MW in FY2025 to 2,400 to 2,500 MW by FY2028 with an investment pipeline of ₹90,000 crore, which works out (our calculation) to roughly ₹72 to 78 crore per MW added.

sections.heading: What moves the number

items: Cooling and density: Anarock maps precision air conditioning (CRAC/CRAH, the most common in India) to 3 to 10 kW per rack, in-row cooling to 15 to 25 kW, rear-door heat exchangers to 20 to 40 kW and direct liquid cooling to 40 to 100 kW or more; it puts an Nvidia H100 GPU cluster at 30 to 60 kW per rack.
Tier and cooling: SBI puts an air-cooled Tier III build at ₹50 to 55 crore per MW and AI with immersion cooling or Tier IV at up to ₹75 crore.
Efficiency targets: SBI reports leading Indian operators at PUE 1.4 to 1.5 and MeitY AI cloud tenders since 2024 requiring below 1.35, which pushes design toward more efficient cooling.

Power infrastructure: Anarock puts DG, UPS, HT supply and switchgear at ₹14 to 22 crore per MW, its largest single line. Ask the discom or transmission utility who pays for the dedicated line, bay and substation.

Crisil says Indian rents are 30 to 35% below peer markets and that contract tenors have lengthened to 15 to 20 years from 10 to 12 years.

title: Data centre site due diligence in India: the feasibility checklist (2026)
description: Due diligence on an Indian data centre site checks title and land use, power evidence, seismic zone, flood and cyclone history, groundwater status, airport height limits and the approvals path.
intro: Due diligence on a data centre site in India answers one question first: can this parcel get the full load, at the voltage needed, on a date you can underwrite? After power come title and land use, groundwater (no new industry other than MSMEs gets a groundwater permit in an over-exploited unit under the 2020 CGWA guidelines), seismic zone under IS 1893, flood and cyclone history from IMD records, AAI height limits within 20 or 56 km of an airport, and the approvals the project will need. NITI Aayog’s October 2026 framework now asks states to verify power and water capacity before clearing data centre projects, so the same questions will come from the state.
takeaways: Power evidence is graded by the document: a written connection offer or sanctioned load beats proximity to a substation.
Groundwater: check the site’s assessment unit category; 730 of 6,762 units (10.8%) were over-exploited in the 2025 assessment.
Seismic: design to IS 1893 (Part 1):2016; BIS lists the 2025 edition of Part 1 as withdrawn.
Airports: AAI height clearance is needed within 20 km of VFR and 56 km of IFR airports; it is valid 8 years and has no fee.

sections.heading: Power evidence: the first and most decisive check

blocks.text: The test is the document behind the MW. A parcel near a 220 kV substation is not a 100 MW site until the utility has said, in writing, how much it can supply and when, and what upgrades that depends on. Crisil estimates that by FY2030 data centre capacity could equal about 60% of Mumbai’s current peak demand and about 80% of Visakhapatnam’s.

sections.heading: Water and groundwater

blocks.text: Under the CGWA guidelines of 24 September 2020, any new or expanding industry or infrastructure project that abstracts groundwater needs a NOC unless exempt, and no new industry other than MSMEs gets one in an over-exploited unit. Infrastructure projects are treated as location specific and are not barred outright. Whether a data centre is treated as industry or infrastructure is not settled in the guidelines’ text, so confirm it with the authority for the specific site.

The 2025 national assessment classed 730 of 6,762 units (10.8%) as over-exploited. Citizen Matters, citing CGWB’s assessment, reports that all 10 assessment units in Bengaluru Urban and Rural districts are over-exploited.

sections.heading: Seismic, flood, cyclone and coast

blocks.text: The IS 1893 (Part 1):2002 town list puts Delhi in zone IV, Mumbai, Chennai, Pune, Kolkata and Ahmedabad in zone III, and Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Visakhapatnam in zone II. Flood records to check against include 944 mm on 26 July 2005 in Mumbai, a 24-hour record for the city, and 1,178.3 mm in November 2015 at Chennai’s Meenambakkam. Cyclone Hudhud crossed the coast over Visakhapatnam on 12 October 2014 with maximum sustained winds of about 180 km/h and a 1.4 m storm surge.

Near the coast, the CRZ Notification 2019 sets a No Development Zone of 200 m from the high tide line in CRZ-IIIB, and of 50 m in CRZ-IIIA (rural areas with more than 2,161 people per sq km) once the coastal zone management plan under the 2019 notification is approved; until then 200 m continues to apply.

sections.heading: Airport height limits

blocks.text: Under G.S.R. 751(E) of 2015, a height clearance from AAI is needed within 20 km of an airport operating under visual flight rules and 56 km of one under instrument flight rules. It is valid for 8 years and has no fee. Navi Mumbai International Airport began commercial flights on 25 December 2025 and Noida International Airport on 15 June 2026; Noida International Airport issued an advisory in July 2025 that no construction should take place within 20 km of it without an AAI height clearance.

title: Data centre land in India: acres per MW, land prices and powered land (2026)
description: Data centre land in India runs ₹3 to 60 crore per acre and about half an acre per MW on Anarock’s bands. Prices, recent deals, data centre parks, FAR rules and what makes land powered.
intro: Data centre land in India costs from about ₹3 crore per acre for 100 to 500 MW parks to ₹35 to 60 crore per acre for small sites in Mumbai’s suburbs, on Anarock’s 2026 benchmarks. Its size bands imply roughly half an acre per MW of IT load (our calculation). Savills counted more than 120 acres of data centre land transacted in H1 2026, as reported by Communications Today. Land becomes powered land only when the utility has committed MW and a date in writing. State authorities such as YEIDA in Uttar Pradesh and MIDC in Maharashtra have dedicated data centre parks or plans for them.
takeaways: Anarock size bands: 5 to 10 MW on 2 to 5 acres, up to 100 to 500 MW on 50 to 200 acres (midpoints about 0.4 to 0.5 acre per MW, our calculation).
Recent deals: STT GDC paid ₹282 crore for 3.48 acres with a building in Navi Mumbai (our conversion from 14,093 sq m); Amazon Data Services paid ₹125.13 crore for 10.6 acres from Lodha.
Parks: YEIDA’s 100-acre Data Centre Park in Sector 28; MIDC data centre parks in Maharashtra; Karnataka’s planned 500 MW park near Hoskote.
Building norms help: Uttar Pradesh (2026) and West Bengal (2021) allow FAR 3.0 plus 1.0 purchasable for data centres.

sections.heading: How much land does a data centre need in India?

columns: Acres per MW at the midpoint (our calculation)

blocks.text: Land per MW is not fixed. The ratio depends on how many storeys the building has, the FAR the state allows, and how much of the site goes to the substation, generators and fuel. Anarock advises buying 30 to 50% more land than phase 1 needs.

sections.heading: Data centre parks in India

items: Uttar Pradesh: YEIDA lists a 100-acre Data Centre Park in Sector 28. UP’s 2026 policy defines a Data Center Park as a data centre with at least 40 MW of total load capacity.
Maharashtra: according to S&R Associates, the IT/ITeS Policy 2023 says MIDC will take up data centre parks with all prior clearances for land allotted to data centres.
Karnataka: Cushman & Wakefield reports a planned 500 MW data centre park near Hoskote, with the government committing solar power and treated water, and 500 MW planned at Mysuru and Mangaluru.
Andhra Pradesh: ETV Bharat reported in October 2025 that the state offered Google’s subsidiary Raiden Infotech a 25% discount on 480 acres across Rambilli, Adavivaram and Mudasarlova, and Tarluvada.
Private parks: Lodha has earmarked 400 acres at Palava for a data centre park, as reported by Business Standard in April 2026.

sections.heading: FAR, ground coverage and stamp duty

blocks.text: Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 policy gives data centres base FAR 3.0 free plus 1.0 chargeable, keeps basement parking, storage and DG space out of FAR, extends service FAR to 40% for DG sets, allows ground coverage of up to 60% or as per byelaws, whichever is higher, and no restriction on floor-to-ceiling height subject to overall height rules. It exempts 100% of stamp duty on land bought or leased from a government authority and gives a land subsidy of 25% of sector rates in the Madhyanchal and Paschimanchal regions (Paschimanchal includes Gautam Buddha Nagar) and 50% in Bundelkhand and Purvanchal.
West Bengal’s 2021 policy also allows FAR 3.0 plus 1.0 purchasable and 60% ground coverage.

sections.heading: Powered land in India

blocks.text: Powered land means land with deliverable electricity for the load, documented by the utility, not land near a substation. In Navi Mumbai, Structure Research reports that the roughly 6 GW MSEDCL allocated to data centres is close to fully committed and that new builds are moving to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani, where separate substations can be commissioned.

title: Seismic zones, flood and cyclone risk for data centres in India (2026)
description: Indian data centre cities by IS 1893 seismic zone, the withdrawn 2025 edition with Zone VI, record rainfall in Mumbai, Chennai and Hyderabad, east coast cyclones and CRZ limits.
intro: Mumbai, Chennai, Pune and Kolkata, which hold about 71% of India’s operational data centre capacity on Cushman & Wakefield’s H1 2026 split (our calculation), are in seismic zone III under the IS 1893 (Part 1):2002 town list, with Delhi in zone IV and Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Visakhapatnam in zone II. A 2025 edition of the code added a Zone VI, but BIS now lists IS 1893 (Part 1):2025 as withdrawn and the 2016 edition as published. Flood risk is the more frequent problem: 944 mm of rain fell on Mumbai on 26 July 2005 and Chennai’s Meenambakkam recorded 1,178.3 mm in November 2015. On the east coast, Cyclone Hudhud crossed Visakhapatnam in 2014 with maximum sustained winds of about 180 km/h.
takeaways: Zone factors in the 2002 town list: 0.10 (II), 0.16 (III), 0.24 (IV), 0.36 (V).
Design to IS 1893 (Part 1):2016; BIS lists the 2025 edition of Part 1, which added Zone VI, as withdrawn.
Chennai and Visakhapatnam carry cyclone exposure; Mumbai and Chennai carry the record rainfall events.
Near the coast, the CRZ 2019 No Development Zone in CRZ-III is 50 m or 200 m from the high tide line.

sections.heading: Seismic zones of India’s data centre cities

blocks.text: City zones and zone factors are from Annex E of IS 1893 (Part 1):2002. Noida and the YEIDA sectors are not listed by name; confirm the zone for a specific site against the edition in force.

sections.heading: The 2025 seismic map and Zone VI

blocks.text: EastMojo reported in November 2025 that the revised code, IS 1893:2025, added a new highest-risk Zone VI and placed the entire Northeast in it. BIS’s programme of work for its earthquake engineering committee now lists IS 1893 (Part 1):2025 among withdrawn or superseded standards and IS 1893 (Part 1):2016 among published standards.
For a data centre project that means designing to the 2016 edition today and watching for a re-issued revision, which could change the zone for sites near zone boundaries.

sections.heading: Flood history in data centre cities

rows: 944 mm, breaking the city’s 24-hour rainfall record
1,178.3 mm in the month at Meenambakkam, the all-time November record
415 mm at Meenambakkam from 3 December to 1.30 pm on 4 December, per IMD figures reported by The News Minute
More than 300 mm within 24 hours in many parts of Hyderabad and Cyberabad

blocks.text: The BMTPC Vulnerability Atlas of India (third edition, 2019) maps flood, cyclone, wind and earthquake hazard by state and district and is a reasonable first screen before site-specific drainage and plinth studies.

sections.heading: Cyclones on the east coast

blocks.text: Very severe cyclonic storm Hudhud crossed the coast over Visakhapatnam between 12:00 and 13:00 IST on 12 October 2014, with maximum sustained winds of about 180 km/h, an estimated central pressure of 950 hPa and a storm surge of 1.4 m above the astronomical tide at the Visakhapatnam tide gauge. With more than 4 GW announced in Visakhapatnam, according to Invest India and Cushman & Wakefield, wind loads, surge level and access after landfall belong in the design basis there.

sections.heading: Heat and coastal limits

blocks.text: Chennai’s Meenambakkam station records a mean daily maximum of 37.3°C in May and 37.2°C in June (1991 to 2020 normals), which sets the cooling design point for the city.

The CRZ Notification 2019 sets a No Development Zone of 200 m from the high tide line in CRZ-IIIB and of 50 m in CRZ-IIIA (rural areas with more than 2,161 people per sq km), the 50 m applying only once the coastal zone management plan under the 2019 notification is approved. Coastal sites near Mumbai, Chennai and Visakhapatnam need the CRZ map checked before layout.

title: Water for data centres in India: groundwater NOC, water stress and state rules
description: Indian data centres need a CGWA or state groundwater NOC to draw groundwater, and new industries are barred in over-exploited units. Water use per MW, water-stressed cities and state incentives.
intro: A data centre in India that draws groundwater needs a NOC from the Central Ground Water Authority or the state groundwater authority under the guidelines of 24 September 2020, and no new industry other than an MSME gets one in an over-exploited unit. Whether a data centre counts as industry or as infrastructure, which is not barred in over-exploited units, has to be confirmed for each site. Anarock puts water use for cooling-tower data centres at about 25.5 million litres per MW per year. SBI names Bengaluru, Chennai and Gurugram as water-stressed data centre metros, and Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 policy directs data centres to adopt closed-loop systems and treated wastewater reuse.
takeaways: CGWA 2020 guidelines: NOC needed for groundwater abstraction by industry and infrastructure, with telemetry flow meters, rooftop rainwater harvesting and, above 100 m3 a day for industries, annual water audits.
Over-exploited units: no NOC for new industries except MSMEs; 730 of 6,762 units (10.8%) were over-exploited in 2025.
Water use: about 25.5 million litres per MW per year for cooling-tower designs (Anarock).

Karnataka’s 2026-31 policy, as reported by The News Minute, reimburses treated water costs; Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 policy requires a water availability assessment before land allocation in state agency areas.

sections.heading: Do data centres need a groundwater NOC in India?

blocks.text: The CGWA guidelines (S.O. 3289(E), 24 September 2020) require all new and existing industries, industries seeking expansion, infrastructure projects and mining projects that abstract groundwater to seek a NOC from CGWA or the state or UT groundwater authority, unless exempt. Exemptions cover domestic users, rural drinking water, the armed forces, agriculture and micro and small enterprises drawing less than 10 m3 a day.

rows: No NOC for any new industry except MSMEs; expansion that increases abstraction is not permitted
Location specific; not barred in over-exploited units, but groundwater for construction only if no treated sewage is available within 10 km
An STP is mandatory for new projects where groundwater need exceeds 20 m3 a day
Digital water flow meter with telemetry, mandatory for all NOC holders
One for 11 to 50 m3 a day; one with a data logger for 51 to 500; two (one with telemetry) above 500
₹20 to ₹200 per m3 for industrial units, depending on the assessment unit category and volume

blocks.text: Whether a data centre is an industry or an infrastructure project under these guidelines is not settled in the text we reviewed. In an over-exploited unit it decides whether a NOC is possible at all, so put the question to the authority before committing to the site.

sections.heading: Water stress in data centre cities

blocks.text: The 2025 Dynamic Ground Water Resources Assessment found 730 of 6,762 assessment units (10.8%) over-exploited. Citizen Matters, citing CGWB’s assessment, reports that all 10 assessment units in Bengaluru Urban and Rural districts are over-exploited, and Newslaundry reported in April 2026 that most of Bengaluru’s data centres sit in its water-stressed areas. Check the category of the unit for a specific site.
SBI names Bengaluru, Chennai and Gurugram as water-stressed data centre metros and notes that newer rules require water management plans.

sections.heading: How much water does a data centre use in India?

blocks.text: Anarock puts water use at about 25.5 million litres per MW per year for data centres with cooling towers.

The design choice drives the number. The government’s September 2026 explainer says AI infrastructure is driving adoption of direct-to-chip liquid cooling, adiabatic cooling and immersion cooling, and that closed-loop liquid cooling systems are emerging as resource-efficient solutions.

sections.heading: State water rules and incentives

items: Uttar Pradesh (2026): in state agency areas, water availability must be assessed before land is allocated, prior permission or a NOC is needed before using water, and data centres shall adopt water-efficient cooling, closed-loop systems and treated wastewater reuse.

Karnataka (2026 to 2031): reimburses 100% of treated water charges up to ₹8 lakh a year for 5 years and offers a water usage effectiveness incentive of up to ₹30 lakh a year for 2 years at a WUE of 0.7 to 1.3 litres per kWh, as reported by The News Minute.
NITI Aayog (October 2026): asks states to verify water capacity before clearing data centre projects.

blocks.text: Operators are moving the same way: Digital Edge announced in February 2026 an 83 MW solar PPA and liquid cooling using 10 million litres of recycled water a day at its BOM campus in Navi Mumbai.

title: Power for data centres in India: grid supply, open access and tariffs by state
description: Data centres in India buy power from the discom, through open access or from captive plants. The routes, connection voltages, tariffs for Tamil Nadu and UP, and partly confirmed rates for three more states.
intro: A data centre in India gets its power from the state distribution company (discom), at a voltage set by the state supply code for its contract demand, and can add renewable power through green energy open access or captive plants. Under the supply codes, loads above about 10 MVA connect at 110 kV to 230 kV; a bulk consumer of 50 MW or more can connect directly to the inter-state grid. Tariffs differ by state: Tamil Nadu charged ₹7.50/kWh plus ₹608/kVA a month from July 2025, and Uttar Pradesh ₹6.10 to ₹7.10/kVAh for 2026-27. The binding question for a site is rarely the tariff: it is whether the substation and line can deliver the MW, and by when.
takeaways: Three routes: discom supply at high or extra high voltage, green energy open access from 100 kW, and captive or group captive generation (26% ownership, 51% consumption).
Maharashtra classifies data centres as industrial by name; Tamil Nadu bills them as IT services under HT-I; Uttar Pradesh covers notified IT units under HV-2.
Load above 10 MVA usually moves to 110 kV, 132 kV or 220 kV supply from a transmission substation, under each state’s supply code.
The Central Electricity Authority estimates data centre demand of about 17 GW by 2031-32.

blocks.text: Most campuses combine the first route with one of the others: the discom supplies the connection, standby and balance, while open access or captive plants provide renewable energy. A bulk consumer of 50 MW or more may instead connect directly to the inter-state transmission system under CERC’s General Network Access regulations.

blocks.text: Each state supply code ties the connection voltage to contract demand. A 20 MW hall and a 200 MW campus therefore connect very differently.

blocks.text: Maharashtra’s numbers need care. MERC revised them in a review order of 25 June 2025, to ₹600/kVA and ₹8.68/kVAh at EHV from 1 July 2025. We have not confirmed whether later orders changed these rates, so check the rate in force with MSEDCL before using any of these figures. The Gujarat row is from one small licensee’s order; we did not confirm that the state discoms use the same schedule.
We have not verified current tariffs for Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Haryana or West Bengal for this guide. For those states, the commission’s latest retail supply tariff order is the source.

sections.heading: Which states treat data centres as industry

items: Maharashtra: MERC classified data centres and semiconductor units as industrial to attract high, continuous loads; industrial incentives apply, and data centres using 100% green power get a 10% discount on wheeling charges.
Tamil Nadu: data centres fall under HT-I as IT services, following the state ICT policy definition.
Uttar Pradesh: the HV-2 industrial category covers IT and ITeS units the state notifies by policy.

blocks.text: State data centre policies add power incentives on top. Odisha’s 2022 policy exempts electricity duty for 10 years up to 5 MVA and subsidises 30% of the power bill for five years, capped at ₹2 crore. Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 policy exempts electricity duty for 10 years. Gujarat’s 2026-29 policy offers a power tariff subsidy of ₹1 per unit for 20 years to eligible projects of 150 MW or more of IT load.

sections.heading: Where power is the constraint

blocks.text: Data centre capacity is still under 1% of India’s installed power capacity, according to the government, but it is concentrated. Structure Research reports that committed and under-construction data centre capacity in Navi Mumbai is approaching the roughly 6 GW of grid capacity MSEDCL allocated there, pushing new builds towards Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani. Crisil Ratings estimates, as reported by Deccan Herald, that by FY2030 data centre capacity could equal about 60% of Mumbai’s current peak demand and about 80% of Visakhapatnam’s.

The Central Electricity Authority has asked states including Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Tamil Nadu to enhance resource adequacy for data centre demand, ThePrint reported in April 2026. The head of TGSPDCL, one of Telangana’s two discoms, told ThePrint that data centres need transmission lines of 132 kV and above.

faqs.question: How do data centres in India get electricity?
faqs.answer: From the state discom, at a voltage set by the state supply code for the contract demand, often supplemented by renewable power bought through green energy open access or from captive plants. Bulk consumers of 50 MW or more can also connect directly to the inter-state grid under CERC rules.

faqs.question: What is the electricity tariff for data centres in India?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and category. Tamil Nadu charged ₹7.50/kWh plus ₹608/kVA a month from July 2025; Uttar Pradesh charges ₹6.10 to ₹7.10/kVAh plus ₹270 to ₹300/kVA for 2026-27; Telangana’s FY 2024-25 order set ₹6.65 to ₹7.65/kVAh plus ₹500/kVA for HT industry. Fuel adjustment, duty and taxes are extra.

faqs.question: Are data centres treated as industrial consumers for power?
faqs.answer: In Maharashtra, yes, by name in the MERC tariff order. Tamil Nadu bills them under HT-I as IT services, and Uttar Pradesh under the HV-2 industrial category for notified IT units.

faqs.question: Can a data center in India buy renewable power directly?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022 allow any consumer with 100 kW or more of contracted demand to buy renewable power through open access, and captive or group captive plants are allowed if the consumer owns at least 26% and uses at least 51% of the output.

faqs.question: How much power will data centres in India need?
faqs.answer: The Central Electricity Authority estimates about 17 GW of data centre demand by 2031-32. Today data centre capacity is less than 1% of installed power capacity.

title: Data centre grid connection in India: voltage by load, dual grid and GNA (2026)
description: How a data centre connects to the grid in India: voltage thresholds in state supply codes, who pays for lines and bays, dual-grid supply, inter-state access from 50 MW and the CERC dual connectivity draft.
intro: A data centre in India connects through the state discom at a voltage its supply code ties to contract demand: in Tamil Nadu 110 kV from 10 to 50 MVA and 230 kV above 50 MVA; in Uttar Pradesh 132 or 220 kV above 10 MVA; in Telangana 132 kV or above beyond 10 to 20 MVA. In the codes we checked, dedicated lines, take-off bays and a second source are paid for by the consumer. Bulk consumers of 50 MW or more can apply for direct connection to the inter-state transmission system, and a CERC draft of 16 June 2026 would let data centres hold both state and inter-state connections for the same load. The date depends on substation and line work the codes do not time-bound.
takeaways: Above roughly 10 MVA, supply moves from 33 kV to 110, 132 or 220 kV from a transmission substation; the exact threshold is in each state’s supply code.

Telangana’s code makes the consumer pay the full cost of a dedicated feeder, including the take-off arrangement at the substation; Maharashtra charges the extra cost of a second source to the consumer.
Bulk consumers of 50 MW and above may connect directly to the inter-state grid under CERC’s 2022 GNA regulations.
CERC’s June 2026 draft on dual connectivity names data centres; CTUIL supported it, Grid-India and CEA opposed it. It is still a draft.

sections.heading: Connection voltage by contract demand, state by state

blocks.text: Maharashtra, MERC Supply Code 2021:
Tamil Nadu, Supply Code categories: 11 or 22 kV up to 3 or 5 MVA depending on the area network, 33 kV up to 10 MVA, 110 kV from 10 to 50 MVA, and 230 kV above 50 MVA.

Uttar Pradesh, Supply Code 2005 as amended: 33 kV from 3,000 to 10,000 kVA and 132 or 220 kV above 10,000 kVA. For developers and colonisers above 10,000 kVA, the code calls for a 132 kV feeder from the nearest 132 or 220 kV substation; a 220 kV feeder from the nearest 220 or 400 kV substation is allowed on request if the licensee considers it essential, with clearances from the transmission licensee where necessary.

sections.heading: Who pays for the line, the bay and a second source

items: Telangana: supply at 132 kV or above is through a dedicated feeder or a loop-in loop-out arrangement decided by the transmission company, and for a dedicated feeder the consumer pays the full cost of the service line, including take-off arrangements at the substation.

Maharashtra: the licensee may provide multiple sources of supply if the consumer asks and it is technically feasible, but the additional cost is borne by the consumer, who may also face additional fixed charges set by the Commission.
Uttar Pradesh: an independent feeder can be given on request if the consumer bears all applicable charges, subject to technical feasibility and availability of a bay and corridor at the substation.

blocks.text: State data centre policies have offered to carry part of this. Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy promised dual power from the grid for sanctioned loads of 50 MW or more and an additional feeder above 100 MW, for projects incorporated up to 31 March 2026. Uttar Pradesh’s 2021 policy gave dual-grid supply to its first three parks, and its 2026 policy subsidises dual-grid supply for parks. Gujarat’s 2026-29 policy facilitates dual feeders.

sections.heading: How long a connection takes

blocks.text: Maharashtra’s code sets timelines: supply from the existing network within 7 to 30 days, three months where mains must be extended or augmented, and one year where a new distribution substation is needed. We found no state code that sets a timeline for a new 132 kV or 220 kV bay or line; in practice that depends on the transmission utility approving and building the scheme.

Maharashtra’s State Grid Code shows the planning tests a new load is checked against: the intra-state system must withstand the outage of a 132 kV or 220 kV double-circuit line, a 400 kV single-circuit line or a single interconnecting transformer without curtailing load, and a single 220 kV substation should not normally exceed 500 MVA, or a 400 kV substation 2,000 MVA.

sections.heading: Direct connection to the inter-state grid and the 2026 draft

blocks.text: CERC’s GNA Regulations 2022 let a bulk consumer seeking to connect directly to the inter-state transmission system, with a load of 50 MW and above, apply for General Network Access. A 2023 amendment lets such a consumer share that access with subsidiaries connected at the same point.

On 16 June 2026 CERC published a draft fourth amendment that would let an entity already connected to a state network also connect directly to the inter-state system for the same drawal capacity, with the state transmission utility’s consent. CERC wrote that data centres, green hydrogen plants and smelters may require dual connectivity with round-the-clock, economical power. The nodal agency would grant access only after technical studies. CTUIL supported the proposal; Grid-India opposed it over control-area and scheduling issues, and CEA opposed it as leading to a sub-optimal transmission system. As of 21 November 2026 we had not seen a final notification.

The same memorandum quotes CTUIL saying it has difficulty finalising transmission for about 33 GW of renewable connectivity partly because of uncertainty in bulk loads like green hydrogen and data centres. For a developer, that is the planning gap in one sentence: transmission for a load gets built when the load is credible on paper.

sections.heading: Data centre parks with their own distribution

blocks.text: Maharashtra’s industries department notified 25 areas in Kurla, Chandivali, Marol, Thane, Navi Mumbai and Panvel as data centre parks and units with deemed distribution licences, and an October 2025 energy department order lets notified parks and units set up captive renewable generation and distribution, as reported by Construction World. Structure Research links the shift to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani to the near-full 6 GW allocation for Navi Mumbai.

sections.heading: Inspection before energisation

blocks.text: Before an installation is energised, the CEA (Measures relating to Safety and Electric Supply) Regulations 2023 apply. Each state notifies the voltage up to which owners may self-certify. Andhra Pradesh set 33 kV in March 2026: installations above 33 kV are inspected by the Electrical Inspector, and generating units above 10 kW need inspection before commissioning. A draft CEA connectivity standard issued in July 2026 would also bring bulk consumers connected at 33 kV and above under common technical standards, as reported by Indian Infrastructure.

faqs.question: At what voltage does a data centre connect in India?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state supply code and the contract demand. In Tamil Nadu, 110 kV from 10 to 50 MVA and 230 kV above 50 MVA; in Uttar Pradesh, 132 or 220 kV above 10 MVA; in Telangana, 132 kV or above beyond 10 MVA on a common feeder or 20 MVA on a dedicated one; in Maharashtra, extra high voltage above 10 MVA (20 MVA in metro areas).

faqs.question: Who pays for a dedicated 132 kV or 220 kV line to a data centre?
faqs.answer: The consumer, in the codes we checked. Telangana’s code makes the consumer pay the full cost of a dedicated feeder including take-off at the substation, and Uttar Pradesh gives independent feeders if the consumer bears the charges and a bay is available.

faqs.question: Can a data centre connect directly to the inter-state transmission system?
faqs.answer: Yes, if its load is 50 MW or more: CERC’s GNA Regulations 2022 let bulk consumers apply for direct connection to the inter-state system. A June 2026 CERC draft would also allow dual state and inter-state connection for data centres; it is not final.

faqs.question: What is dual grid supply for a data centre?
faqs.answer: Supply from two independent sources so one outage does not drop the site. Maharashtra allows it on request with the extra cost borne by the consumer; Tamil Nadu’s 2021 and Uttar Pradesh’s data centre policies offered it to large loads and parks.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get a power connection for a data center in India?
faqs.answer: Maharashtra’s code sets one year where a new distribution substation is needed. No state code we found sets a timeline for a new 132 kV or 220 kV bay or line, which depends on the transmission utility building the scheme.

steps.name: Fix the load and phasing
steps.text: Set the contract demand per phase; it decides the connection voltage under the state supply code.

steps.name: Find the connection point
steps.text: Identify the discom or transmission substations that can supply the load at that voltage and the line route to the site.

steps.name: Apply to the discom
steps.text: Apply for the new connection; above about 10 MVA the discom and state transmission utility decide the substation, bay and feeder arrangement.

steps.name: Decide on dual supply and inter-state access
steps.text: Request a second source if needed, at the consumer’s cost in the codes we checked; loads of 50 MW or more may apply for direct inter-state access under CERC’s GNA rules.

steps.name: Build or pay for the dedicated line and bay
steps.text: In the codes we checked, dedicated feeders and take-off bays are paid for by the consumer.

steps.name: Inspect and energise
steps.text: Get the Electrical Inspector’s approval or self-certify within the state’s notified voltage under the CEA safety regulations 2023, then energise.

title: Green energy open access for data centres in India: rules, banking and ISTS (2026)
description: How data centres in India buy renewable power: Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022 (100 kW, 15-day deemed approval, monthly banking), the ISTS waiver phase-out to 2028, and group captive rules amended in March 2026.
intro: Data centres in India buy renewable power mainly through green energy open access and captive or group captive plants. The Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022 open the route to any consumer with 100 kW or more of contracted demand, deem an application approved after 15 days, allow at least monthly banking of at least 30% of consumption, and remove additional surcharge for consumers paying fixed charges. The waiver of inter-state transmission charges for new solar and wind is being phased out, with full charges from July 2028. Captive rules amended in March 2026 keep the 26% ownership and 51% consumption tests and make it easier to hold plants through group companies.
takeaways: Eligibility: 100 kW of contracted demand or sanctioned load; no limit for captive consumers.

The rules list transmission, wheeling, cross subsidy surcharge and standby charges and, since January 2023, banking charges and fees such as load despatch, scheduling and deviation settlement charges; no additional surcharge if fixed charges are paid.
ISTS charges for solar and wind commissioned after 30 June 2025 rise from 25% to 100% by July 2028.
Captive and group captive avoid cross subsidy surcharge and additional surcharge if the 26% and 51% tests are met.

sections.heading: What the Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022 allow

rows: Consumers with contracted demand or sanctioned load of 100 kW and above; no limit for captive consumers
Within 15 days, failing which it is deemed approved; applications through a central nodal agency portal
At least monthly, of at least 30% of the total monthly consumption from the discom
Transmission, wheeling, cross subsidy surcharge and standby charges; no other charges (widened by the January 2023 amendment, below)
For green energy bought from a renewable plant, cannot rise during 12 years from the plant’s operation by more than 50% of the surcharge fixed for the year open access is granted
Not applicable to green open access consumers paying fixed charges

blocks.text: An amendment of 27 January 2023 (G.S.R. 59(E)) raised the cap on standby charges from 10% to 25% of energy charges and added banking charges and other fees and charges, such as load despatch centre fees, scheduling charges and deviation settlement charges, to the list. The commission fixes the banking charge: in Maharashtra it is 8% of the energy banked, adjusted in kind, as set out in an MSEDCL commercial circular of September 2024.

sections.heading: The inter-state transmission charge waiver and its phase-out

blocks.text: The Ministry of Power extended the waiver of inter-state transmission charges to solar and wind projects commissioned up to 30 June 2025. After that the waiver steps down by commissioning year, running July to June: projects commissioned from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026 pay 25% of the charges, 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027 50%, 1 July 2027 to 30 June 2028 75%, and from 1 July 2028 100%. The ministry describes this as a waiver reducing by 25% a year after 30 June 2025, lasting 25 years from commissioning. The same 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% steps appear in the ministry’s order for new hydro projects, keyed there to the dates of contract award and PPA signing.
For a data centre signing a long-term renewable contract now, the commissioning date of the generator decides how much of the inter-state charge the contract carries for its life.

sections.heading: Captive and group captive under the 2026 amendment

blocks.text: The Electricity (Amendment) Rules 2026, notified in March 2026, amend Rule 3 of the Electricity Rules 2005. The tests stay at 26% ownership and 51% of the electricity generated consumed by captive users. Ownership now counts subsidiaries, the holding company and fellow subsidiaries, and verification moves to NLDC for inter-state cases.

pv magazine India summarises the other changes: a special purpose vehicle is treated as an association of persons whose members can meet the tests together; each user’s consumption is capped at its proportionate ownership share unless it holds 26% or more; and cross subsidy and additional surcharges are not levied pending verification, with carrying cost if the plant later fails the tests.

sections.heading: State green power terms that matter to data centres

items: Maharashtra: green tariff of ₹0.25/kWh over the category tariff for the fifth control period (FY 2025-26 to FY 2029-30), and a 10% wheeling discount for data centres using 100% green power; MERC rejected a zero green tariff for round-the-clock green power to data centres.
Gujarat 2026-29 policy: at least 51% renewable power for eligible projects; open access is allowed.
Uttar Pradesh 2026 policy: promotes 50% renewable energy adoption in new data centres by 2030, and offers transmission and wheeling exemptions of up to 100% depending on the renewable source.
Odisha 2022 policy: 100% reimbursement of transmission and wheeling charges for captive renewable power within the state.

sections.heading: What operators have signed

blocks.text: Digital Edge signed a solar power purchase agreement with Hexa Climate for up to 83 MW for the first phase of its Navi Mumbai campus, with power delivered in phases from December 2026. Meta, alongside leasing capacity at Reliance’s 168 MW Jamnagar facility, contracted nearly 1 GW of new renewable capacity with CleanMax and Fourth Partner Energy, TechCrunch reported. The Star reported in May 2026 that STT GDC and Nxtra source about 40% of their energy from non-fossil sources.

CERC framed its June 2026 draft on dual connectivity around round-the-clock and economical power for data centres and similar loads, which would let a site draw renewable power over the inter-state grid and firm it from the state network. Nuclear is the longer option: the draft SHANTI Rules of August 2026 would license captive nuclear generation and name data centres as a use. Both are drafts.

faqs.question: What is green energy open access?
faqs.answer: The route under the Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022 that lets a consumer with 100 kW or more of contracted demand buy renewable power from a generator of its choice over the grid, with approval deemed after 15 days and charges limited to those the rules list.

faqs.question: Can data centres use green energy open access in India?
faqs.answer: Yes. Any consumer with 100 kW or more of contracted demand is eligible, and captive consumers have no limit. Data centres in Maharashtra using 100% green power also get a 10% wheeling discount.

faqs.question: What charges apply under green energy open access?
faqs.answer: Transmission, wheeling, cross subsidy surcharge, standby and banking charges, plus fees such as load despatch, scheduling and deviation settlement charges. Additional surcharge does not apply if the consumer pays fixed charges, and the cross subsidy surcharge cannot rise by more than 50% over 12 years.

faqs.question: What is group captive power?
faqs.answer: Generation owned jointly by its users. Under Rule 3 of the Electricity Rules 2005, as amended in March 2026, users must together own at least 26% and consume at least 51% of the annual output; meeting the tests avoids cross subsidy and additional surcharges.

faqs.question: When does the ISTS waiver for renewable energy end?
faqs.answer: Solar and wind commissioned up to 30 June 2025 keep the full waiver. Later projects pay 25%, 50% and 75% of the charges in successive July to June years, and 100% from 1 July 2028.

title: Open access charges by state in India: cross subsidy surcharge and wheeling (2026)
description: What cross subsidy surcharge, additional surcharge, wheeling, transmission, standby and banking charges are, the caps in the 2022 green open access rules, and the state data centre policy waivers we could verify.
intro: A data centre buying power through open access in India pays the network and the discom for the power it no longer buys from them: transmission and wheeling charges for using the wires, a cross subsidy surcharge and often an additional surcharge to compensate the discom, plus standby and banking charges. The Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022 cap what green open access consumers can be charged: no additional surcharge if they pay fixed charges, and a cross subsidy surcharge that cannot rise by more than 50% over 12 years. The figures themselves are set every year in each state commission’s tariff order, and several state data centre policies waive part of them.
takeaways: Cross subsidy surcharge compensates the discom for the cross subsidy it loses when a consumer buys elsewhere; additional surcharge covers fixed costs stranded by its obligation to supply.
Green open access consumers paying fixed charges do not pay additional surcharge.
Captive and group captive users meeting the 26% and 51% tests pay neither surcharge.

Data centre policy waivers vary: Uttar Pradesh 2026 up to 100% of transmission and wheeling depending on the renewable source; Odisha 100% for in-state captive renewables; Tamil Nadu’s 2021 concessions applied to data centres incorporated up to 31 March 2026.

faqs.question: What is cross subsidy surcharge in open access?
faqs.answer: A charge an open access consumer pays the discom for the cross subsidy the discom loses when that consumer buys power elsewhere. The state commission sets it under Section 42(2) of the Electricity Act 2003; for green open access it cannot rise by more than 50% over 12 years.

faqs.question: What is additional surcharge in open access?
faqs.answer: A charge under Section 42(4) of the Electricity Act 2003 that covers the discom’s fixed costs arising from its obligation to supply. Under the Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022 it does not apply to green open access consumers who pay fixed charges.

faqs.question: What are wheeling charges?
faqs.answer: Charges for using the discom’s distribution network to carry power from the generator to the consumer, set in the state tariff order. In Maharashtra the March 2025 multi-year order set the HT wheeling component at ₹0.62/kVAh for FY 2025-26, since revised by review orders (current rate not verified), with a 10% discount for data centres on 100% green power.

faqs.question: Do data centres pay cross subsidy surcharge on captive power?
faqs.answer: Not if the plant meets the captive tests: at least 26% ownership and at least 51% of annual generation consumed by captive users, under Rule 3 as amended in March 2026.

faqs.question: Which states waive open access charges for data centres?
faqs.answer: Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 policy exempts transmission and wheeling up to 100% depending on the renewable source; Odisha’s 2022 policy reimburses them for in-state captive renewables; Tamil Nadu’s 2021 concessions applied to projects incorporated up to 31 March 2026.

title: India data centre power demand to 2032: what CEA and the government project
description: Official projections of data centre electricity demand in India range from 13.56 GW to 26.3 GW by 2031-32, with CEA at about 17 GW. Why they differ, how they compare with peak demand, and where the load concentrates.
intro: The Central Electricity Authority estimates data centre power demand in India at about 17 GW by 2031-32, the figure the government gave Parliament in August 2026. Other official figures differ: 13.56 GW by 2031-32 was cited in March 2026, and, as reported by Business Standard, the Minister of State for Power told Parliament in July 2026 that AI data centres would add 26.3 GW by 2031-32. Today data centre capacity is under 1% of installed power capacity, against an all-India peak that reached 256.1 GW in April 2026. The load is concentrated: Crisil Ratings estimates data centre capacity could equal about 60% of Mumbai’s current peak demand by FY2030.
takeaways: CEA: about 17 GW of data centre demand by 2031-32 (PIB, August 2026).
Government figures range from 13.56 GW to 26.3 GW for the same year, depending on scope and date.
All-India peak demand: 250 GW (May 2024), 256.1 GW (April 2026), and a reported 270.82 GW (May 2026).
Locally the share is large: Crisil Ratings puts data centre capacity at about 60% of Mumbai’s and about 80% of Visakhapatnam’s current peak by FY2030.

sections.heading: Estimates disagree: the official numbers side by side

rows: About 17 GW of data centre demand
