Minister of State for Electronics and IT, citing Ministry of Power data (March 2026)
Reported by PSU Watch and Business Standard
More than 13.6 GW, and 16.4 GW by 2040
CEA National Generation Adequacy Plan, March 2026
26.3 GW of additional AI data centre load
Minister of State for Power, written reply to Parliament (July 2026)

blocks.text: The figures do not all measure the same thing: the 26.3 GW figure is additional load from AI data centres, while the others are for data centre demand. They also date from different months of 2026. Business Standard reported that the 26.3 GW figure is nearly double the March estimate and is expected to be served primarily by renewable energy capacity.

sections.heading: How that compares with India’s power system

rows: 256.1 GW (solar 21.5% of supply at the peak)
Data centre share of installed capacity

blocks.text: The Ministry of Power’s year-end review gave 242.49 GW as the FY 2025-26 maximum, while its April 2026 release cites 245.4 GW on 9 January 2026; we use the later figure. The 270.82 GW peak was reported by ANI, citing the Ministry of Power; we did not find a PIB release for it. CEA’s mid-term review of the 20th Electric Power Survey projects all-India peak demand of 388 GW in 2031-32, as reported by Business Standard.

sections.heading: Where the load lands

blocks.text: National shares understate the local effect. Crisil Ratings estimates, as reported by Deccan Herald, that by FY2030 data centre capacity could equal about 60% of Mumbai’s current peak demand, about 20% of Hyderabad’s and about 80% of Visakhapatnam’s. The Star reported in May 2026 that data centres could consume a third of the electricity produced in Mumbai by 2030.

Cushman & Wakefield counted 1,789 MW of operational capacity in the top seven cities in H1 2026, with Mumbai holding 890 MW, and 3,860 MW of upcoming supply expected by 2030. Structure Research reports that committed and under-construction capacity in Navi Mumbai is approaching the roughly 6 GW of grid capacity MSEDCL allocated to data centres there.

sections.heading: How planners are responding

items: CEA set up a committee on the operational, policy and regulatory issues of large data centres, their grid impact and cybersecurity, reporting to the National Power Committee (KNN India, October 2026).
CEA asked states including Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Tamil Nadu to enhance resource adequacy for data centre demand (ThePrint, April 2026).
CERC’s June 2026 draft would let data centres hold both state and inter-state connections; CTUIL cites uncertainty in data centre loads as one reason transmission planning is stuck.

S.K. Soonee, founding CEO of POSOCO, and Parikshit Pareek of IIT Roorkee have urged that data centre load characteristics, such as planned IT load, PUE and UPS configuration, be integrated into CEA’s transmission and distribution planning criteria.

blocks.text: Nuclear is part of the government’s answer: in his August 2026 Independence Day address the Prime Minister linked chips, AI and data centres to electricity demand and the SHANTI Act, with a 100 GW nuclear target for 2047.

title: Power study for a data centre site in India: load flow and N-1 against the grid
description: What a power study for an Indian data centre site covers: the discom, state and inter-state network, load flow and N-1 tests to state grid code criteria, what data is public, and what only the utility confirms.
intro: A power study for a data centre site in India estimates how many MW each nearby substation can take, at which voltage, and what limits it, by modelling the discom, state transmission (STU) and, for 50 MW and above, inter-state (CTU) network around the site and testing it at N-0 and N-1. The test criteria come from the state grid code: Maharashtra’s requires the system to withstand the loss of a 132 kV or 220 kV double-circuit line, a 400 kV single circuit or a single interconnecting transformer without load curtailment. A screening study tells you where to apply, how much to ask for and which upgrades to expect. Only the discom’s sanction, or the nodal agency’s grant of inter-state access, makes a number firm.
takeaways: The study follows the connection hierarchy: 33 kV discom supply for small halls, 110 to 230 kV STU substations above about 10 MVA, and inter-state access for 50 MW and above.
State grid codes set the N-1 tests and substation limits; in Maharashtra a single 220 kV substation should not normally exceed 500 MVA, or a 400 kV substation 2,000 MVA.
Public network data in India is thinner than the planning question needs; we found no CTUIL plan naming transmission schemes for the main data centre clusters.
The utility’s own approval is what makes the MW and the date firm.

sections.heading: What the study covers

rows: Discom 33 kV and STU 66 to 400 kV substations, lines and transformers around the site for each study year, with inter-state elements where the load may connect at 400 kV
Each substation that could supply the load at the voltage its contract demand falls under in the state supply code, plus line-in line-out options
Peak and light-load conditions, near-term and later years, with other announced data centre and industrial loads in and out
AC load flow at N-0 and N-1 to the state grid code criteria, for example loss of a 220 kV double-circuit line or an interconnecting transformer
Thermal and voltage limits, the element that binds first and at what MW, and substation capacity limits in the grid code
The augmentation that lifts each limit, an indicative cost range and an energisation range, with the approvals each depends on

blocks.text: The method is the same as a US utility-grade study; what changes is the hierarchy of who studies and approves the connection, and the planning criteria each state sets.

sections.heading: The planning tests a new load must pass

blocks.text: Maharashtra’s State Grid Code 2020 requires the intra-state transmission system to withstand, without load curtailment, the outage of a 132 kV double-circuit line, a 220 kV double-circuit line, a 400 kV single-circuit line or a single interconnecting transformer. The outage of one transformer at a 66 kV or higher substation must not overload the rest, and new substations can be proposed when urban transformers exceed 70% loading. A single substation should not normally exceed 250 MVA at 132 kV, 500 MVA at 220 kV or 2,000 MVA at 400 kV.

For inter-state access, bulk consumers of 50 MW or more apply for GNA to the nodal agency, the Central Transmission Utility, under CERC’s GNA regulations. CERC’s June 2026 draft amendment would grant GNA to entities seeking dual connectivity, such as data centres, only after the nodal agency carries out technical studies.

sections.heading: What data is public, and what is not

items: Public: state supply codes and grid codes, tariff orders, CERC regulations and drafts, and the transmission utilities’ published plans.

Thin: the CTUIL rolling plan study report we retrieved for 2026-27 does not mention data centres, and we found no CTUIL or Grid-India document naming schemes for the Navi Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad or Visakhapatnam clusters.
Moving: CEA set up a committee on data centres and grid stability in 2026, and NITI Aayog has asked states to verify power and water capacity before clearing projects.

blocks.text: That gap is why a screening study in India leans on the substation and line data that can be assembled, the announced loads competing for the same substation, and direct questions to the discom and STU.

sections.heading: Why AI loads change the study

blocks.text: S.K. Soonee, founding CEO of POSOCO, and Parikshit Pareek of IIT Roorkee have written that a voltage disturbance can trigger data centre protection that shifts load to backup, and that such silent exits can remove gigawatts of load in seconds, producing frequency overshoot. They argue that data centre load characteristics, such as planned IT load, PUE, UPS configuration, backup mode and commissioning timelines, should be integrated into CEA’s transmission and distribution planning criteria, and that interconnection standards should require voltage ride-through. A draft CEA connectivity standard of July 2026 would bring bulk consumers at 33 kV and above under common technical standards.

sections.heading: What makes a number firm

blocks.text: A screening study does not commit a discom or transmission utility to anything. The number becomes firm when the discom sanctions the load and the STU approves the substation and bay works, or, for inter-state access, when the nodal agency grants GNA. The study’s value is in arriving at that application with the right connection point, the right MW and the right questions.

title: Diesel generator rules for data centres in India: CPCB IV, consents and PESO (2026)
description: Which rules govern data centre backup generators in India: CPCB IV norms for sets up to 800 kW, older standards above 800 kW, the genset-based pollution category, PESO diesel storage thresholds and Delhi NCR curbs.
intro: Backup generators at an Indian data centre answer to three sets of rules: engine emission norms, the state pollution board’s consent category, and petroleum storage licensing. Emission limits notified by G.S.R. 804(E) of 3 November 2022, which CAQM calls CPCB IV, apply to new genset engines up to 800 kW from 1 July 2023; diesel engines above 800 kW fall under standards notified in 2002. Under CPCB’s January 2025 classification, a data centre whose only pollution source is gensets is Orange if it has 1 MVA or more on liquid fuel and Green if on gaseous fuel. If the diesel stored is Class B petroleum (confirm the class with PESO), storage above 2,500 litres needs a licence and above 25,000 litres a PESO licence.
takeaways: G.S.R. 804(E) (CPCB IV) sets emission limits for new genset engines up to 800 kW from 1 July 2023.
Diesel engines above 800 kW are covered by concentration-based standards notified in 2002 and regulated by state pollution control boards.
Genset capacity and fuel decide the pollution category: 1 MVA or more on liquid fuel is Orange; on gaseous fuel, Green.
For Class B petroleum (confirm the class with PESO): no licence below 2,500 litres, district licence to 25,000 litres, PESO licence above.

sections.heading: Emission norms for data centre gensets

blocks.text: Emission limits for new genset engines up to 800 kW were notified by G.S.R. 804(E) of 3 November 2022 and apply from 1 July 2023, as reported by SCC Online; CAQM refers to these standards as CPCB IV. For engines up to 800 kW, compliance is certified at manufacture: CPCB’s system and procedure provides for a type approval certificate and conformity of production certificates for each engine family.

Standards notified in 2002 (G.S.R. 489(E)); for sets commissioned from 1 July 2005: CO 150 mg/Nm3, NMHC 100 mg/Nm3, PM 75 mg/Nm3 on diesel, NOx 710 ppm(v), or 360 ppm(v) in larger plants
Regulated by the state pollution control board

blocks.text: The NOx limit for sets above 800 kW depends on the total engine rating of the plant and the area category; check the CPCB standard for the version that applies to a given site.

sections.heading: Pollution category and consent

blocks.text: CPCB’s January 2025 classification says projects such as data centres whose pollution potential comes only from gensets may be classified by genset capacity and fuel. Gensets totalling under 1,000 kVA may not need additional classification. Gensets totalling 1 MVA or more on liquid fuel are Orange (pollution index 60.0); on gaseous fuel, Green (50.5). Separately, a building construction project of 20,000 sq m or more of built-up area is Orange.

CPCB says the classification may be used for consent management and inspection frequency, and generator buildings appear in environmental clearances for large campuses: one 2025 Maharashtra clearance covered two data centre buildings, two DG buildings and a substation. Gas gensets are therefore a consent question as well as a fuel question.

blocks.text: PESO lists diesel (HSD) among products that need a licence under the Petroleum Rules 2002. Class B covers flash points from 23°C to below 65°C; confirm the class of the fuel specified for the site with PESO before relying on these thresholds.

sections.heading: Delhi NCR and the Graded Response Action Plan

blocks.text: In Delhi NCR, the Commission for Air Quality Management regulates the use of DG sets, particularly during restrictions under the Graded Response Action Plan. Its schedule, as summarised by the Delhi Pollution Control Committee in June 2025, places no restriction, even under GRAP, on gensets of up to 800 kW that meet the G.S.R. 804(E) standards. title: National data centre policy in India: the 2020 draft and what applies now (2026)
description: India has no notified national data centre policy as of November 2026. The 2020 MeitY draft never came into effect and talks reopened in August 2025. What applies instead, and what to watch.
intro: India does not have a notified national data centre policy. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) issued a Draft Data Centre Policy in November 2020, and it was never notified. MeitY reopened consultations in August 2025, and we found no notified final policy when we checked on 21 November 2026. Until there is one, national rules for data centres come from infrastructure status (October 2022), the Budget 2026-27 tax holiday for foreign cloud companies using Indian data centres, and data protection and localisation law. Several states have their own data centre policies with exemptions and incentives.
takeaways: The 2020 MeitY draft was never notified; consultations restarted in August 2025.
Data centres with a minimum capacity of 5 MW of IT load have had infrastructure status since 11 October 2022.
Foreign cloud companies that procure data centre services in India are exempt on that income from tax year 2026-27 to tax year 2046-47.
NITI Aayog released a Data Centre Evaluation Framework on 14 October 2026; it describes itself as guidance.
Several states have their own data centre policies with exemptions and incentives.

sections.heading: Status of national data centre policy, November 2026

rows: No notified final policy found as of 21 November 2026
Harmonised Master List, notification of 11 October 2022, minimum 5 MW of IT load
Enacted; the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Act 2026, which eases its conditions, received assent on 17 August 2026

About 1,575 MW installed (Rajya Sabha reply, 7 August 2026)
A parliamentary committee report quotes MeitY as keeping no official capacity data

sections.heading: The 2020 draft and the 2025 consultation

blocks.text: MeitY issued the Draft Data Centre Policy in November 2020 and took feedback from stakeholders. It was never notified and never came into effect.

MeitY reopened consultations on a national policy in August 2025. As reported by BW Legal World at the time, the framework under discussion included four Data Centre Economic Zones, single-window clearance and growth in tier 2 and tier 3 cities. In September 2025 Business Standard reported that the draft proposed a tax exemption of up to 20 years for data centre developers that meet capacity, power usage effectiveness and employment targets. Neither has been published as policy.

sections.heading: What applies nationally while there is no policy

items: Infrastructure status: a data centre housed in a dedicated or centralised building with a minimum capacity of 5 MW of IT load is an infrastructure sub-sector under the Communication category of the Harmonised Master List, notified on 11 October 2022.

Tax holiday: foreign companies that provide cloud services globally using data centre services procured in India are exempt on that income from tax year 2026-27 to tax year 2046-47, and must serve Indian customers through an Indian reseller.
Foreign investment: law firms read the FDI policy as allowing 100% foreign investment under the automatic route in companies engaged only in the data centre business.

Data law: RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and CERT-In rules keep defined data and logs in India; under the DPDP Rules 2025 the government can require significant data fiduciaries to keep specified personal data in India from 13 May 2027.

items.label: Infrastructure status, tax holiday and DC SEZs

sections.heading: NITI Aayog's Data Centre Evaluation Framework (October 2026)

blocks.text: NITI Aayog's Frontier Tech Hub released a Data Centre Evaluation Framework on 14 October 2026. It asks for a centralised audit mechanism with MeitY as the nodal ministry, a State-wise Data Centre Approval Matrix in each state, one digital interface for clearances, a citation for every incentive (enabling notification, validity and responsible department), and design-stage assessment of PUE, WUE and CUE against published BIS standards with post-commissioning measurement.

As reported by ThePrint, the framework also asks states to verify grid, water and land capacity before clearing projects and proposes bringing data centres under the Essential Services Maintenance Act. It is not binding.

sections.heading: What the government says about capacity and power

blocks.text: In a Rajya Sabha reply on 7 August 2026, the government said installed data centre capacity grew from 375 MW in 2020 to about 1,575 MW. It named Mumbai, Navi Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Delhi NCR and Jamnagar as the main locations and Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal as states where the industry is expanding. It said data centre capacity is less than 1% of installed power capacity and that the Central Electricity Authority estimates data centre power demand at about 17 GW up to 2031-32.

A parliamentary committee report quoted MeitY as saying that "officially, no data is maintained in MeitY regarding the capacity of Data Centres". Cushman & Wakefield put operational colocation and hyperscale cloud capacity at 1,789 MW in H1 2026.

sections.heading: What to watch next

items: Notification of a final national data centre policy, and whether it creates Data Centre Economic Zones.
Rules or schemes issued for the data centre tax exemption after the August 2026 amendment.
Significant data fiduciary notifications and cross-border transfer rules under the DPDP framework, which apply from 13 May 2027.
State renewals: the Tamil Nadu 2021 policy covered data centres incorporated up to 31 March 2026, and the West Bengal 2021 policy was valid for five years from September 2021.

title: Data centre incentives in India: infrastructure status, tax holiday and SEZs (2026)
description: Central incentives for data centres in India: infrastructure status for 5 MW+ IT load since October 2022, the tax holiday to 2047 for cloud services, FDI rules, and what the SEZ changes do not cover.
intro: At the national level, an Indian data centre gets three things. Since 11 October 2022, a data centre with a minimum capacity of 5 MW of IT load is an infrastructure sub-sector. From tax year 2026-27 to tax year 2046-47, foreign companies that provide cloud services globally using data centre services procured in India are exempt from Indian tax on that income, under the Finance Act 2026; the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Act 2026, which received assent on 17 August 2026, eased its conditions. And law firms read the FDI policy as allowing 100% foreign investment under the automatic route for companies engaged only in the data centre business.
takeaways: Infrastructure status needs a dedicated or centralised building and a minimum capacity of 5 MW of IT load.
The tax holiday benefits the foreign cloud company; profits of the Indian data centre company and the reseller remain taxable.
The August 2026 amendment drops the notification and approved-scheme conditions and extends the holiday to data centres leased and operated by an Indian company.
The June 2025 SEZ land relaxations cover semiconductor and electronic component manufacturing; data centres are not among the listed sectors.

sections.heading: Central incentives at a glance

rows: Easier access to institutional credit at lower rates (PTI report)

Exemption on a foreign company’s income from data centre services procured in India

sections.heading: Infrastructure status under the Harmonised Master List

blocks.text: The Ministry of Finance added data centres to the Harmonised Master List of Infrastructure Sub-sectors, under Communication, by a notification dated 11 October 2022. The entry covers a "Data Centre housed in a dedicated/centralized building for storage and processing of digital data applications with a minimum capacity of 5 MW of IT load."
According to a PTI report at the time, the move helps data centre companies get easier access to institutional credit at lower rates and attract foreign investment.

sections.heading: The tax holiday to 2047 for cloud services delivered from India

blocks.text: The Budget of 1 February 2026 proposed a tax holiday till 2047 for foreign companies providing cloud services to customers globally using data centre services from India, with services to Indian customers provided through an Indian reseller entity. It also proposed a safe harbour of 15% on cost where the Indian data centre service provider is a related entity. Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said investments of around USD 70 billion were underway and around USD 90 billion had been announced.

The government backgrounder sets the window at tax year 2026-27 to tax year 2046-47 and says profits from domestic activity, including data centre services provided by the resident Indian data centre company and resale by the Indian reseller, remain taxable.

The Finance Act 2026, notified on 30 March 2026, exempts a foreign company’s income "by way of procuring data centre services from a specified data centre", if the foreign company is notified by the central government, does not own or operate the physical infrastructure or resources of the data centre, sells to users in India only through an Indian reseller company and furnishes prescribed information. A specified data centre had to be set up under an approved scheme, notified by MeitY, and owned and operated by an Indian company.

The Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 passed the Lok Sabha on 6 August and the Rajya Sabha on 10 August 2026, and received the President’s assent on 17 August 2026. It removes the conditions that the foreign company be notified and that the data centre be set up under an approved scheme and notified, and extends the exemption to data centres leased and operated by an Indian company. Check any rules or schemes issued under it before relying on the amended conditions.

sections.heading: Foreign investment in data centres

blocks.text: As Khaitan & Co read the FDI policy, 100% foreign investment is allowed under the automatic route in Indian companies or LLPs engaged only in the data centre business. If the company is also in other businesses, for example owning fibre assets, the investment conditions for those sectors apply as well. S&R Associates notes that investors from restricted countries (Pakistan, Afghanistan, Nepal, Bhutan, China including Hong Kong, Bangladesh and Myanmar) need prior government approval.

sections.heading: SEZs, GIFT City and data embassies

blocks.text: The SEZ (Amendment) Rules 2025, in effect from 3 June 2025, cut the minimum land requirement for semiconductor and electronic component manufacturing units in SEZs from 50 hectares to 10 hectares. The sectors listed, such as semiconductors, printed circuit boards, lithium-ion cells and IT hardware components, do not include data centres.

In the Budget 2023-24 speech the Finance Minister said that, for countries looking for digital continuity solutions, the government would facilitate data embassies in GIFT IFSC. DD India reports that Gujarat’s 2026 data centre policy document highlights Dholera and GIFT City among the state’s industrial hubs.

title: DPDP Act and data localisation: what it means for data centres in India (2026)
description: India's DPDP Act 2023 restricts transfers by a negative list, not blanket localisation. RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, CERT-In and telecom licences do require data in India. What each means for data centres.
intro: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 does not require all personal data to stay in India. Section 16 lets the central government restrict transfers to countries it notifies, and keeps stricter laws on transfer in force. The DPDP Rules 2025, notified in November 2025 with an 18-month phased timeline, let the government require significant data fiduciaries to keep specified personal data in India; according to Taxmann, that rule and Section 16 apply from 13 May 2027. Localisation already comes from sector rules: RBI for payment system data since 2018, SEBI for regulated entities’ cloud data since 2023, IRDAI for insurance-sector logs and data, and CERT-In for logs.
takeaways: DPDP Section 16 is a negative list: transfers are allowed unless a country is notified.
Section 16 and the Rules on significant data fiduciaries and cross-border transfer apply from 13 May 2027, according to Taxmann.
RBI requires the entire payment system data to be stored only in India.
SEBI regulated entities must keep cloud data, including DR and logs, within India.
CERT-In requires 180 days of ICT logs kept within India and five years of subscriber records at data centres.

sections.heading: Which rules keep data in India

rows: The entire data relating to payment systems, including end-to-end transaction details
Data and processing, including DC, DR, near-DR and logs; PaaS and SaaS only in MeitY-empanelled data centres with a valid STQC audit status
IRDAI Information and Cyber Security Guidelines, 24 April 2023
All ICT infrastructure logs, critical and business data (entities other than insurers); insurers under separate record-keeping rules
Service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporates and government organisations
ICT logs for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction
Subscriber accounting information and user information, with listed exceptions
Nothing by default; transfers to notified countries can be restricted
Act of 11 August 2023; section applies from 13 May 2027
Personal data the government specifies on a committee’s recommendation, with its traffic data

sections.heading: What the DPDP Act says about cross-border transfer

blocks.text: Section 16(1) of the Act says the central government "may, by notification, restrict the transfer of personal data by a Data Fiduciary for processing to such country or territory outside India as may be so notified." Section 16(2) keeps any other law that provides "a higher degree of protection for or restriction on transfer", so sector rules such as RBI’s continue to apply on their own terms.

Section 10 lets the government notify significant data fiduciaries on factors including the volume and sensitivity of data, risk to the rights of data principals, sovereignty and integrity of India, electoral democracy, security of the State and public order. They must appoint a Data Protection Officer based in India and an independent data auditor, and carry out periodic data protection impact assessments and audits. The highest penalty in the Schedule, up to ₹250 crore, is for failing to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a personal data breach.

sections.heading: The DPDP Rules 2025 and the May 2027 date

blocks.text: PIB announced on 14 November 2025 that the government had notified the DPDP Rules 2025 with an 18-month phased compliance timeline. Consent managers must be Indian companies, data fiduciaries must respond to data principal requests within a maximum of 90 days, and significant data fiduciaries "must also comply with government-specified restrictions on certain categories of data, including localisation where required."

Under the Rules, a significant data fiduciary must ensure that personal data specified by the central government, on the recommendation of a committee, and the traffic data relating to its flow are not transferred outside India. Taxmann, in an analysis updated on 15 November 2026, gives 13 May 2027 as the date from which this rule and Section 16 apply.
In January 2026 Business Standard reported that MeitY had proposed cutting the implementation period for certain provisions for significant data fiduciaries from 18 to 12 months.

sections.heading: Sector rules that already require data in India

blocks.text: RBI’s circular of 6 April 2018 requires all system providers to ensure that "the entire data relating to payment systems operated by them are stored in a system only in India", including full end-to-end transaction details. The foreign leg of a transaction may also be stored abroad.

SEBI’s cloud framework of 6 March 2023 says "the data should reside/be processed within the legal boundaries of India", covering DC, DR, near-DR and logs. For PaaS and SaaS, regulated entities may only choose providers that host and process their data within data centres empanelled by MeitY and holding a valid STQC audit status.

IRDAI’s guidelines of 24 April 2023 require regulated entities other than insurers to store all ICT infrastructure logs, critical and business data in India. Insurers must store primary data in India under separate guidelines and regulations. IRDAI issued amendments to the guidelines on 6 April 2026; confirm whether the localisation clause changed.

CERT-In’s directions of 28 April 2022 require cyber incidents to be reported within 6 hours and ICT logs to be kept for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction. Data centres, VPS, cloud and VPN providers must also keep validated subscriber records for 5 years or longer.

Telecom licensees may not transfer subscriber accounting information or user information outside India, with exceptions for international roaming, billing and IPLC subscribers, under clause 39.23(viii) of the Unified Licence.

sections.heading: What this means for data centre demand and design

items: Payment system providers, SEBI regulated entities and insurance-sector regulated entities must keep defined data in India; for SEBI regulated entities this includes DR and near-DR copies.
Operators that want SEBI-regulated PaaS and SaaS workloads need MeitY empanelment and a valid STQC audit status for the facility.
CERT-In names data centres directly: log retention, incident reporting and subscriber records are duties of the facility, not only of its tenants.
The DPDP Act alone does not force localisation today. Watch for significant data fiduciary notifications and any restricted-country list.

faqs.question: Does the DPDP Act require data localisation in India?
faqs.answer: Not by default. Section 16 allows transfers unless the government notifies a country as restricted, and keeps stricter laws such as RBI’s payment data rule in force.

faqs.question: When do the DPDP Rules 2025 come into force?
faqs.answer: In phases over 18 months from their notification in November 2025. According to Taxmann, Section 16 and the Rules on significant data fiduciaries and cross-border transfer apply from 13 May 2027.

faqs.question: Do payment companies have to store data in India?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under RBI’s 2018 circular the entire data relating to payment systems must be stored only in India.

faqs.question: Can SEBI regulated entities use cloud data centres outside India?
faqs.answer: No. SEBI’s 2023 framework requires the data, including DR and logs, to reside and be processed within India.

faqs.question: What does CERT-In require from a data centre in India?
faqs.answer: Incident reports within 6 hours, ICT logs for 180 days kept within India, and validated subscriber records for 5 years or longer.

faqs.question: Does a data centre need MeitY empanelment?
faqs.answer: For SEBI regulated entities, yes in one case: PaaS and SaaS providers serving them must host and process their data only in data centres empanelled by MeitY and holding a valid STQC audit status.

title: Data centre policy in India: state data centre policies compared (2026)
description: Which Indian states have a data centre policy in 2026, which have lapsed, and what each offers on capital subsidy, power tariff, stamp duty and open access. A dated state by state table with sources.
intro: India has no notified national data centre policy, and several states have their own. As of 21 November 2026, Uttar Pradesh (2026), Gujarat (2026 to 2029), Maharashtra (IT/ITES Policy 2023 and the Integrated Green Data Centre Parks policy of October 2024), Andhra Pradesh (4.0, 2024 to 2029) and Odisha (2022) have published data centre policies or policy chapters. Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy covered data centres incorporated up to 31 March 2026 and West Bengal’s 2021 policy was valid for five years from September 2021; we found no successor to either. Invest India and Cushman & Wakefield counted eleven states with dedicated data centre policies in force as of September 2026.
takeaways: Invest India and Cushman & Wakefield counted 11 states with dedicated data centre policies in force as of September 2026.
Eligibility thresholds differ widely: 150 MW of IT load in Gujarat, ₹500 crore of eligible fixed assets in Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy, above 2 MW for UP data centre units.
Green power conditions differ: Gujarat requires 51% renewable power for core operations (law-firm summary); Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy required at least 30%.

Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 policy classifies the data centre industry as an essential service under ESMA, and Gujarat’s 2026 policy does the same according to a law-firm summary; West Bengal’s 2021 policy did too, but its five-year term has ended.
Mumbai held about 50% of India’s operational data centre capacity in H1 2026, according to Cushman & Wakefield.

sections.heading: Essential service status

blocks.text: Uttar Pradesh’s 2026 policy says the data centre industry in the state has been classified under ESMA as an essential service provider. Gujarat’s 2026 policy treats data centre operation, management, maintenance and support as an essential service under the Gujarat Essential Services Maintenance Act, 1972, according to Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas; we have not seen the notified resolution. West Bengal’s 2021 policy says data centre organisations "shall be classified under ‘Essential Services’", though that policy’s five-year term has ended.
NITI Aayog’s October 2026 framework proposes bringing data centres under the Essential Services Maintenance Act. It is not binding.

sections.heading: Lapsed, replaced and unclear policies

items: Tamil Nadu: the 2021 policy applies to data centres incorporated from 1 April 2021 until 31 March 2026. We found no successor as of 21 November 2026.
West Bengal: the 2021 policy was valid for five years from 6 September 2021 or until replaced. In May 2026 the state BJP president said the government was working on a new data centre policy.

Uttar Pradesh: the 2026 policy repealed the 2021 policy (First Amendment 2022). Holders of a Letter of Comfort under the old policy that have availed incentives remain eligible for the admissible benefits.

Telangana: the state has announced a target of five gigawatts of hyperscale capacity by 2029 (Deccan Chronicle). For Amazon’s Hyderabad project it allocated 202 acres in Bharat Future City and 98 acres in Chandanvelly, with incentives worth ₹125 crore (ThePrint).
Karnataka: MediaNama reported in September 2026 that the cabinet approved a Sustainable Data Centre Policy 2026-31 with a budget framework of ₹1,300.45 crore. We had not seen the notified text.

sections.heading: Which state is best for a data centre?

blocks.text: It depends on size and location more than on headline incentives. Gujarat’s policy only admits projects of 150 MW or more. Uttar Pradesh has a band for units above 2 MW. Mumbai had 890 MW of operational capacity in H1 2026, about 50% of the national total (Cushman & Wakefield), but Structure Research reports that MSEDCL has allocated about 6 GW of grid power to data centres in Navi Mumbai and that committed and under-construction capacity is approaching that level.

Check three things before choosing on incentives: whether the policy is in force on the date your project is registered, whether your load and investment clear its threshold, and whether the power path to the site can deliver the MW on your date.

title: Uttar Pradesh data centre policy 2026: parks, capital subsidy and power incentives
description: The UP Data Centre Policy 2026 runs five years from notification: interest subsidy up to ₹50 crore for parks, capital subsidy up to ₹20 crore and a 10-year electricity duty exemption for units, and wheeling relief.
intro: Uttar Pradesh replaced its 2021 data centre policy with the UP Data Centre Policy 2026, notified by a government order of 9 July 2026 and in effect for five years from notification. It aims for an additional 2 GW or more of capacity and more than ₹2 lakh crore of investment, and classifies projects as parks of at least 40 MW, units above 2 MW and below 40 MW, and edge data centres. Parks can get an interest subsidy up to ₹50 crore and a dual-grid power subsidy; units can get a capital subsidy of 7% up to ₹20 crore and a 10-year electricity duty exemption. Wheeling and transmission charges are exempted by 50% to 100% for 25 years, depending on how the power is bought. Cushman & Wakefield counted 156 MW of operational data center capacity in Noida in mid-2026.
takeaways: The 2026 policy repealed the 2021 policy; Letter of Comfort holders that have already availed incentives under it remain eligible for the admissible benefits.
Land subsidy is 25% of sector rates in Madhyanchal and Paschimanchal and 50% in Bundelkhand and Purvanchal, on land bought or leased from state agencies.
Stamp duty is 100% exempt on purchase or lease from government authorities, against a bank guarantee released at commercial operation.
The policy aims for at least 50% renewable energy in new data centres by 2030.
Projects above ₹200 crore are approved by the State Cabinet on the recommendation of the Empowered Committee.

sections.heading: Incentives by segment

items: Parks of 40 MW or more: interest subsidy of 60% of annual interest for 7 years, capped at ₹10 crore a year and ₹50 crore in total, and reimbursement of the cheaper of two grid connections, for the first eight parks or an added 2 GW, whichever comes first.

Units above 2 MW and below 40 MW: capital subsidy of 7% of eligible fixed capital investment up to ₹20 crore, paid over 10 years, and 100% electricity duty exemption for 10 years from commercial operation.

Parks and units: land subsidy of 25% in Madhyanchal and Paschimanchal and 50% in Bundelkhand and Purvanchal on land from state agencies; 100% stamp duty exemption on purchase or lease from government authorities and 50% on the second transaction (park to unit), granted against a bank guarantee released at commercial operation.
Boosters: an AI Compute Booster, a green operations booster tied to certification, PUE and renewable share, and reimbursement of Tier III and Tier IV certification charges.

blocks.text: The government order adds a non-financial chapter covering essential service status under ESMA, water supply, building norms and electricity supply. Projects above ₹200 crore are approved by the State Cabinet on the recommendation of the Empowered Committee.

sections.heading: Power: electricity duty, wheeling and dual grid

blocks.text: Units get a 100% electricity duty exemption for 10 years. Transmission and wheeling charges are exempted for 25 years from commissioning: 50% on intra-state purchase, 75% on renewable power from within the state, and 100% of intra-state charges on inter-state purchase, for the first eight parks or an added 2 GW. Parks get the dual-grid subsidy, and the policy aims for at least 50% renewable energy in new data centres by 2030.
Incentives do not create grid capacity. A park still needs a connection the distribution company or transmission utility can deliver on its date.

sections.heading: What the 2021 policy offered, and who keeps it

blocks.text: The 2021 policy targeted 250 MW, ₹20,000 crore and at least three private parks. It offered units a capital subsidy of 7% up to ₹10 crore and parks an interest subsidy of 60% for 7 years up to ₹50 crore per park, plus land subsidy of 25% or 50% up to ₹75 crore, stamp duty exemption of 100% on the first transaction and 50% on the second, electricity duty exemption for 10 years for units, dual grid for the first three parks with the Energy Department bearing the cost of the second grid, and 50% transmission and wheeling exemption for 25 years on intra-state sale.

The 2022 amendment raised the targets to 900 MW, ₹30,000 crore and at least eight parks. The 2026 policy repeals the 2021 policy and its amendment; entities holding a Letter of Comfort under it that have partly or fully availed incentives remain eligible for the admissible benefits.

sections.heading: Where Uttar Pradesh’s data centres are

blocks.text: Cushman & Wakefield counted 156 MW of operational capacity in 12 data centres in Noida in mid-2026, with 21 MW under construction, 223 MW planned and 1,247 MW at an early stage. Delhi NCR as a whole had 183 MW operational.

intro: Maharashtra has no standalone data centre policy. At ₹60,000 crore or more, parks also get an industrial incentive grant of 75% of eligible fixed capital investment, according to the same analysis.

title: Tamil Nadu data centre policy: the 2021 policy, incentives and status (2026)
description: Tamil Nadu's Data Centre Policy 2021 covered data centres incorporated up to 31 March 2026, with a ₹500 crore minimum and 30% renewable power. We found no successor as of November 2026.
intro: Tamil Nadu’s Data Centre Policy 2021 came into force on 23 November 2021 and applies to data centres incorporated from 1 April 2021 until 31 March 2026. Incentives needed eligible fixed assets of at least ₹500 crore and at least 30% renewable energy, and included a 100% electricity tax subsidy for five years, open access charges at 50%, a concessional cross subsidy surcharge and dual grid supply for loads of 50 MW or more. The policy is administered by ELCOT. As of 21 November 2026 we found no successor policy, so a data center project incorporated after 31 March 2026 should confirm its position with the state before relying on these terms.
takeaways: The eligibility window closed on 31 March 2026; no successor was found by 21 November 2026.
Captive data centres were excluded.
Loads of 50 MW or more got power from two grids, and loads above 100 MW an additional feeder.
Chennai had 214 MW operational in mid-2026, about 12% of the top seven cities.

title: Telangana data centre policy: the 2016 policy, incentives and Hyderabad (2026)
description: Telangana adopted its Data Centres Policy in 2016, and no newer policy was found by November 2026. The state targets 5 GW of hyperscale capacity by 2029, and Hyderabad has India’s second-largest pipeline.
intro: Telangana issued its Data Centres Policy in 2016, which Cushman & Wakefield describes as the first dedicated state data centre policy in India, and we found no newer data centre policy or government order as of 21 November 2026. The state government has announced a target of 5 GW of hyperscale data centre capacity by 2029, according to Deccan Chronicle. Large projects have received project-specific incentives: according to ThePrint, Amazon was allocated 202 acres in Bharat Future City and 98 acres in Chandanvelly with incentives worth ₹125 crore. The state targets 5 GW of hyperscale capacity by 2029, according to Deccan Chronicle.
South Hyderabad held 634 MW planned and 1,758 MW at an early stage in mid-2026.
AWS holds 46% of Hyderabad’s live IT capacity, according to Knight Frank’s 2025 market update.

title: Gujarat data centre policy 2026-29: 150 MW threshold and ₹1 per unit subsidy
description: The Viksit Gujarat Data Centre Policy 2026-29, launched 9 July 2026, targets 7.5 GW: 150 MW minimum IT load, 51% renewable power, ₹1 per unit for 20 years and 20 years of electricity duty reimbursement.
intro: Gujarat launched the Viksit Gujarat Data Centre Policy 2026-29 on 9 July 2026 and issued its Government Resolution on 7 August 2026, with a target of 7.5 GW and about ₹6 lakh crore of investment. It is in force for three years from notification, extendable, and incentives stop once 7.5 GW is installed. Only projects with an approved IT load of at least 150 MW qualify, and at least 51% of power for core operations must be renewable. According to Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas, incentives include a ₹1 per unit power tariff subsidy for 20 years, 100% electricity duty reimbursement for 20 years, an interest subsidy of up to 4% for 10 years, stamp duty exemption and SGST reimbursement, capped at 75% of eligible fixed capital investment, and data center operations are treated as an essential service under the Gujarat Essential Services Maintenance Act, 1972. These terms are as reported by a law firm and the press; we have not seen the notified Government Resolution.
takeaways: The 150 MW threshold makes this a policy for large campuses, not for small colocation sites.
Eligible fixed capital investment excludes land, land development and chips and is capped at the lower of 80% of fixed capital investment or ₹60,000 crore per GW.
Battery storage counts for at most 10% of the capital subsidy.
The policy document highlights Dholera and GIFT City, and the state announced two planned cable landing stations in Gujarat.
Gujarat incentives cannot be combined with other Gujarat policies, but central schemes are allowed.

title: Karnataka data centre policy 2026-31: incentives, water rules and the 2022 policy
description: Karnataka’s cabinet approved a Sustainable Data Centre Policy 2026-31 in September 2026: ₹1,300.45 crore budget, 1 GW target, PUE incentive up to ₹20 crore and parks at Hoskote, Mangaluru and Mysuru.
intro: Karnataka’s cabinet approved a Sustainable Data Centre Policy 2026-31 in September 2026, with a budget framework of ₹1,300.45 crore and a target of 1 GW of cumulative IT load by 2031, according to MediaNama. It links incentives to energy and water efficiency: up to ₹20 crore for a PUE of 1.00 to 1.20 sustained for three years, water use reimbursements and support for treated water, according to The News Minute. It proposes parks at Hoskote, Mangaluru and Mysuru on 30 plus 30 year leases with dual-grid power. We had not seen the gazette notification as of 21 November 2026. The earlier Karnataka Data Centre Policy 2022 gave capital, land and stamp duty support to data center projects outside Bengaluru.
takeaways: The 2026-31 policy links incentives to measured PUE and water use effectiveness.
Water use effectiveness of 0.7 to 1.3 litres per kWh earns reimbursement of water charges up to ₹30 lakh a year for two years.
Projects above ₹3,000 crore can get custom packages, including for cable landing stations and desalination.
Bengaluru had 162 MW operational in mid-2026.

title: Andhra Pradesh data centre policy 4.0 (2024-29): incentives and mega projects
description: Andhra Pradesh notified its Data Center Policy 4.0 on 14 November 2024. Projects above 50 MW can get tailor-made packages; in 2026 the state cleared four projects with ₹2.83 lakh crore of proposed investment.
intro: Andhra Pradesh notified its Data Center Policy (4.0) 2024-29 through G.O.Ms.No.6 of the IT, Electronics and Communications Department on 14 November 2024. It is valid for five years from notification, or until a new policy is announced, whichever is later. Standard incentives are a choice between 100% net SGST reimbursement on capital goods and a 10% capital subsidy on plant and machinery, plus 100% stamp duty exemption on first sale and industrial power tariff. Projects above 50 MW, or above ₹5,000 crore of fixed capital investment in plant and equipment, can get tailor-made incentives case by case. In 2026 the state issued orders for four projects under the policy with ₹2,83,340 crore of proposed investment. Google’s first India AI hub, about USD 15 billion over 2026 to 2030, is in Visakhapatnam.
takeaways: Standard incentives: 100% net SGST reimbursement on capital goods or a 10% capital subsidy on plant and machinery.
The August 2026 order for ReNew’s 1,000 MW project in Anakapalli caps its fiscal incentives at a combined ₹14,405 crore.
Crisil estimates Visakhapatnam data centre capacity could equal about 80% of the city’s current peak power demand by fiscal 2030.

title: Haryana data centre policy 2026: capex and opex support and the 2022 policy
description: Haryana notified its Data Centre Policy 2026 on 27 May 2026 for five years, with capex and opex support for hyperscale data centres above 10 MW and core data centres above 1 MW and up to 10 MW.
intro: Haryana notified the Haryana Data Centre Policy 2026 in the state gazette on 27 May 2026 (notification No. 20/12/2026-4IB-1). It is valid for five years, or until a new policy or amendment, whichever is earlier, and targets ₹10,000 crore of investment. Hyperscale data centres above 10 MW get capex reimbursement of 20% up to ₹25 crore per unit and opex reimbursement of 50% up to ₹8 crore a year for five years; core data centres of more than 1 MW and up to 10 MW get 10% up to ₹1 crore per MW and 30% up to ₹4 crore a year. Units that began operating after 7 July 2022 and before the 2026 policy fall under the Haryana State Data Centre Policy 2022. Gurugram had 18 MW of operational data center capacity in mid-2026.
takeaways: Categories: hyperscale above 10 MW; core above 1 MW and up to 10 MW; units need at least 1 MW and parks at least 20 MW.
Edge data centres (300 kW to 1 MW) are supported under the Haryana Progressive MSME and Exports Policy 2026 instead.
The policy records that data centres were declared an essential service under the Haryana Essential Services Maintenance Act, 1974, in July 2023.

title: Madhya Pradesh data centre policy: IT, ITeS and ESDM Policy 2023 incentives (2026)
description: We found no standalone Madhya Pradesh data centre policy as of November 2026. Data centres fall under the IT, ITeS and ESDM Investment Promotion Policy 2023, which gives anchor data centres 25% capex support.
intro: We found no standalone data centre policy in Madhya Pradesh as of 21 November 2026. Data centres are covered by a chapter of the state’s IT, ITeS and ESDM Investment Promotion Policy 2023, issued by the Department of Science and Technology on 29 September 2023 for five years or until a new policy, whichever is earlier. The first five anchor data centres with at least ₹500 crore of gross fixed capital investment can get 25% capex assistance up to ₹125 crore each, and the first five data centres of at least 5 MW get a power tariff reimbursement of ₹2 per unit for five years. The central government named Madhya Pradesh among states coming up as new data centre investment destinations in August 2026, and CtrlS broke ground on a data centre in Bhopal in April 2025.

Data centre units after the first five anchors get 15% capex assistance up to ₹50 crore and ₹1 per unit tariff reimbursement.

title: Data centres in Mumbai and Navi Mumbai: capacity, sub-markets and power (2026)
description: Mumbai had 890 MW of operational data centre capacity in H1 2026, about half of India’s top seven cities, most of it on Thane-Belapur Road in Navi Mumbai, where grid allocation is now the constraint.
intro: Mumbai is India’s largest data centre market. Cushman & Wakefield counted 890 MW of operational capacity in Mumbai in H1 2026, about 50% of the top seven cities, with 281 MW under construction and 1,445 MW planned. Thane-Belapur Road in Navi Mumbai holds 675 MW of it, and the city has 13 cable landing stations. Structure Research reports that MSEDCL has allocated about 6 GW of grid capacity to Navi Mumbai data centres, that committed and under-construction capacity is approaching that figure, and that new builds are moving to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani.

Thane-Belapur Road holds 675 MW at 4.4% colocation vacancy. Powai holds 176 MW. Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani are where new builds are moving, per Structure Research.
Structure Research reports that committed capacity is approaching the roughly 6 GW grid allocation for Navi Mumbai data centres. Power evidence is the first check on any Mumbai site.

blocks.text: Estimates differ by method. Cushman & Wakefield counts colocation and hyperscale cloud capacity in the top seven cities. Savills counts IT load. Anarock gives 812 MW IT across 54 facilities for Mumbai-MMR. Use one publisher consistently when comparing periods.

Mumbai took about 83% of capacity added across the top seven cities in H1 2026 (148 MW), and Cushman & Wakefield expects the city to cross 1 GW of operational capacity by the end of 2026. According to Tele.net, the Mumbai Metropolitan Region handles around 95% of India’s international bandwidth.

sections.heading: Sub-markets: Thane-Belapur Road, Powai, Panvel, Taloja and Palava

rows: 241 MW under construction, 995 MW planned, 2,286 MW early stage
40 MW under construction, 185 MW planned, 171 MW early stage

blocks.text: Anarock describes Navi Mumbai (Airoli, Ghansoli, Rabale, Mahape and Panvel) as the largest concentration of hyperscale and colocation data centres, and the Chandivali and Powai-Andheri (E) corridor as a major interconnection hub. Equinix opened MB3 in Chandivali, Powai, in April 2026 with an initial investment of over US$95 million. Anarock names Dombivali and Taloja as an emerging lower-cost hyperscale corridor.

Yotta’s NM1 at Panvel has 52 MW of IT load in a park it says can scale to 1 GW. AdaniConneX lists 1,000 MW of potential capacity in Navi Mumbai, and CoreWeave plans a 240 MW deployment at AdaniConneX’s Taloja campus, with the first phase expected in mid-2028. Digital Edge plans a 400 MW Navi Mumbai campus. STT GDC broke ground at Palava with an initial 50 MW on 46 acres, designed to scale to about 400 MW.

sections.heading: Power: the Navi Mumbai allocation and what comes next

blocks.text: Structure Research reports that MSEDCL has allocated about 6 GW of grid capacity to data centres in Navi Mumbai and that committed and under-construction capacity is approaching that figure. New builds are moving to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani, where separate substations can be commissioned. The same report notes a Maharashtra framework from October 2025 that lets data centre parks generate and distribute their own power.

Crisil Ratings estimates that by fiscal 2030 data centre capacity in Mumbai could equal about 60% of the city’s current peak power demand. That is the scale problem a new site has to answer: a firm date for a large load needs a named substation, a transmission plan and a connection agreement.

Under MERC’s Supply Code, 33 kV supply covers contract demand up to 10,000 kVA, or 20,000 kVA in a Metropolitan Area or on an express feeder; larger loads connect at extra high voltage. A connection that needs a new distribution substation has a one-year standard. Multiple sources of supply can be provided if the consumer asks and it is technically feasible, with the extra cost borne by the consumer.

MERC’s March 2025 tariff order classified data centres in the industrial category, with the same rebates and incentives, and approved a 10% discount in wheeling charges for data centres on 100% green power. Construction World reported in October 2025 that the state industries department had notified 25 areas in Kurla, Chandivali, Marol, Thane, Navi Mumbai and Panvel as designated data centre parks and units with deemed distribution licences.

Maharashtra’s IT/ITES Policy 2023 gives new data centre units outside Zone I a Rs 1 per unit tariff subsidy for 5 years, and a notification of 22 June 2026 exempts data centre units from electricity duty for 20 years. According to a Fox Mandal analysis published by the International Bar Association, a June 2026 government resolution amended the Integrated Green Data Centre Parks policy: at least 51% green power for core operations, and a Rs 1 per unit tariff subsidy for 10 or 20 years depending on investment size.

sections.heading: Land: prices, parcels and approvals

blocks.text: Anarock benchmarks land at Rs 35 to 60 crore per acre for 5 to 10 MW facilities in Mumbai-MMR suburbs and Rs 3 to 10 crore per acre for 100 to 500 MW parks in locations such as Navi Mumbai. Recent deals show the spread. Communications Today reported that STT GDC paid Rs 282 crore for a 14,093 sq m plot (about 3.5 acres) with an existing building in the TTC Industrial Area in May 2026. DCD reported in 2024 that AWS bought 38.18 acres from Lodha at Palava for more than Rs 450 crore.

Building approvals include state environmental clearance. Nxtra’s Mahape expansion in the TTC Industrial Area, with two data centre buildings, two generator buildings and a substation building and 76,930 sq m of total built-up area, received its clearance from SEIAA Maharashtra on 21 November 2025.
Maharashtra’s IT/ITES Policy 2023 gives a 100% stamp duty exemption on land or premises for new or expanded data centres and allows data centres in any zone.

sections.heading: Site risks in Mumbai

items: Seismic: Mumbai and Thane are Zone III (zone factor 0.16) in the IS 1893 (Part 1):2002 town list.
Flood: 944 mm of rain fell on Mumbai on 26 July 2005, breaking the city’s 24-hour record and causing massive flooding (NOAA). Low-lying plots need a site-level drainage and flood check.

Airports: AAI height NOCs apply up to 20 km from VFR airports and 56 km from IFR airports, measured from the aerodrome reference point; where a colour-coded zoning map exists, local bodies can approve heights below its limit. Navi Mumbai International Airport began commercial operations on 25 December 2025.

blocks.text: Invariant checks the evidence behind a site’s power (the DISCOM or transmission connection, the open access route, the nearest substations and what else is queued on them), screens seismic zone, flood history, groundwater status and airport height limits, and lists the central and state approvals the project needs with the authority behind each one. In Mumbai the first question is which substation serves the plot and how much of its allocation is already committed.

title: Data centres in Chennai: capacity, Ambattur, Siruseri and flood risk (2026)
description: Chennai had 214 MW of operational data centre capacity in H1 2026 (Cushman & Wakefield), mostly in Ambattur and Siruseri, with cable landings, high vacancy and a state policy that covered projects incorporated to 31 March 2026.
intro: Chennai is India’s second-largest data centre market by both Cushman & Wakefield’s and Savills’ counts. Cushman & Wakefield counted 214 MW operational in H1 2026 across 18 facilities, about 12% of the top seven cities, with 26.7% colocation vacancy after significant new supply. Savills counts 320 MW IT. Most capacity is in Ambattur in the west and Siruseri on the OMR. The city has 7 cable landing stations with 2 under construction. Tamil Nadu’s Data Centre Policy 2021 applies to data centres incorporated from 1 April 2021 until 31 March 2026.
takeaways: Chennai had 214 MW operational, 55 MW under construction and 313 MW planned in H1 2026 (Cushman & Wakefield). Savills counts 320 MW IT; Anarock 298 MW IT.
Colocation vacancy was 26.7% in H1 2026, against 7.9% in Mumbai. Siruseri vacancy was 41.7%.
Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy applies to data centres incorporated from 1 April 2021 to 31 March 2026. Check what applies to a later project before relying on any incentive.
Meenambakkam recorded 1,178.3 mm in November 2015, its all-time record monthly total for November.

Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy says the state has the second-highest number of submarine cable landing stations in India.

Cushman & Wakefield attributes the high vacancy largely to significant supply entering the market in recent quarters, notes a large GPU deployment by a neocloud provider in H1 2026, and expects hyperscaler and neocloud deployments to raise occupancy. JLL says Chennai accounted for 50% of India’s H1 2026 supply additions in its count.

sections.heading: Sub-markets: Ambattur, Siruseri and the Sriperumbudur corridor

rows: 42 MW under construction, 124 MW planned, 548 MW early stage

blocks.text: Ambattur, in the city’s west, is where large new buildings are going. CapitaLand Data Centre Chennai 01 in Ambattur, with 34 MW of IT capacity, is due for completion by the end of 2026. Lumina CloudInfra, which AirTrunk has acquired, bought 16 acres in Ambattur for a campus with an initial 216 MW of IT load. Siruseri hosts Equinix CN1, opened in September 2025 with 800 cabinets of initial capacity, and campuses from STT GDC and Sify.

Anarock identifies the Oragadam industrial belt and the Parandur-Sriperumbudur corridor as the emerging and long-term growth zone, with larger and cheaper land. Digital Connexion, the Reliance, Brookfield and Digital Realty joint venture, launched its first Chennai campus in January 2024 with capacity for up to 100 MW of critical IT load.

sections.heading: Power and the Tamil Nadu policy after March 2026

blocks.text: The 2021 policy gave incentives to projects investing above Rs 500 crore that meet at least 30% of their energy use from renewable sources. It offered a 100% electricity tax subsidy for 5 years, open access charges at 50% of the conventional charge, a concessional cross subsidy surcharge, dual power from two grids for sanctioned loads of 50 MW or more, and an additional feeder above 100 MW.

Under the Tamil Nadu supply rules, loads from 10 MVA up to 50 MVA are supplied at 110 kV and loads above 50 MVA at 230 kV. TNERC’s tariff order of June 2025 sets HT-I (industries, factories and IT services, which include data centres) at Rs 7.50 per kWh and Rs 608 per kVA per month from 1 July 2025; check for later revisions.

The policy applies to data centres incorporated from 1 April 2021 until 31 March 2026. Projects incorporated after that date should not assume these terms apply. ELCOT drafted the policy; confirm with the state what is available now, and get it in writing.

sections.heading: Land in Chennai

blocks.text: Anarock’s national benchmarks put land for 10 to 30 MW facilities at Rs 5 to 20 crore per acre, varying by state and zone, and land for 100 to 500 MW parks, in locations including outer Chennai, at Rs 3 to 10 crore per acre. Lumina’s 16 acres in Ambattur were reported at over Rs 500 crore in January 2026.

SIPCOT and ELCOT industrial land and private land follow different routes. Whether a separate land-use conversion is needed depends on the parcel; confirm it with the allotting agency or district authority before signing.

sections.heading: Site risks in Chennai: flood, cyclone and water

items: Flood: Meenambakkam recorded 1,178.3 mm in November 2015, its all-time record monthly total for November. During Cyclone Michaung, Meenambakkam received 415 mm from 3 December to 1.30 pm on 4 December 2023, per The News Minute.
Seismic: Chennai is Zone III (zone factor 0.16) in the IS 1893 (Part 1):2002 town list.
Heat: the 1991 to 2020 mean daily maximum at Meenambakkam is 37.3 degrees C in May, which sets the cooling design point.

Water: SBI names Bengaluru, Chennai and Gurugram as water-stressed metros where data centre water use is under scrutiny. Under CGWA guidelines, new industries other than MSMEs cannot get groundwater NOCs in over-exploited assessment units.

blocks.text: Invariant checks the evidence behind a site’s power (the DISCOM or transmission connection, the open access route, the nearest substations and what else is queued on them), screens seismic zone, flood history, groundwater status and airport height limits, and lists the central and state approvals the project needs with the authority behind each one. In Chennai, plot elevation and drainage relative to the 2015 and 2023 flood extents come before anything else.

title: Data centres in Hyderabad: capacity, hyperscalers and power (2026)
description: Hyderabad had 151 MW of operational data centre capacity in H1 2026 and the second-largest pipeline in India after Mumbai, with AWS building at Bharat Future City and Microsoft’s new India South Central region.
intro: Hyderabad has India’s second-largest data centre pipeline after Mumbai. Cushman & Wakefield counted 151 MW operational in H1 2026, about 8% of the top seven cities, but 668 MW planned and 18% of all upcoming supply to 2030, second only to Mumbai. AWS launched its Hyderabad region in November 2022 and has started a greenfield campus at Bharat Future City, and Microsoft launched its India South Central region in Hyderabad on 21 September 2026. Telangana adopted a dedicated data centre policy in 2016, and officials have cited about 5 GW by 2029 or 2030.
takeaways: Hyderabad had 151 MW operational, 42 MW under construction and 668 MW planned in H1 2026 (Cushman & Wakefield).
South Hyderabad holds 92 MW at 0% colocation vacancy, with 1,758 MW at early stage. West Hyderabad holds 59 MW.
Knight Frank puts the committed and early-stage pipeline at about 1.9 GW and says AWS holds 46% of live IT capacity.
Hyderabad is Seismic Zone II, the lowest zone in the IS 1893 (Part 1):2002 scheme. The October 2020 floods are the main recent hazard event.

CtrlS plans a 40-acre park at Chandanvelly Industrial Park with over 600 MW of potential IT load and 250 MW of sanctioned power for phase one.

blocks.text: Crisil Ratings estimates that by fiscal 2030 data centre capacity in Hyderabad could equal about 20% of the city’s current peak power demand, a third of the share it projects for Mumbai. CtrlS reports 250 MW of sanctioned power for the first phase of its Chandanvelly park, an example of the document a buyer should ask to see.

Telangana’s supply rules put contracted demand above 10,000 kVA on a common feeder, or above 20,000 kVA on a dedicated feeder, at 132 kV or above. Supply at 132 kV or above is through a dedicated feeder or a loop-in loop-out arrangement decided by TS Transco, and a consumer on a dedicated feeder pays the full cost of the service line. HT industrial supply at 132 kV and above was Rs 6.65 per kVAh with a Rs 500 per kVA monthly demand charge in the FY 2024-25 order; The Hans India reported no tariff hike for 2026-27.

Cushman & Wakefield notes that Telangana was the first state to implement a dedicated data centre policy, in 2016. ThePrint reported that the state’s land allocations to Amazon came with incentives worth Rs 125 crore.

items: Seismic: Hyderabad is Zone II (zone factor 0.10) in the IS 1893 (Part 1):2002 town list, the lowest zone in that scheme.

Groundwater: under CGWA guidelines, new industries other than MSMEs cannot get groundwater NOCs in over-exploited assessment units. Check the specific unit before relying on borewells.
Airport: Anarock cites airport proximity as an advantage of the southern corridor. AAI height NOCs apply up to 20 km from VFR airports and 56 km from IFR airports.

In Hyderabad the questions are which substation serves the corridor, what is already allocated on it, and the height surface over the plot.

Seismic Zone IV (Delhi, IS 1893 Part 1:2002); Noida International Airport height limits

blocks.text: Anarock counts 179 MW IT across 18 facilities and forecasts 550 MW by 2030.

sections.heading: Sub-markets: Noida Expressway, Greater Noida, YEIDA and Gurugram

blocks.text: Anarock’s zones include the Noida Expressway corridor (Sectors 62, 132, 142, 143 and 150 to 167), the Greater Noida corridor (Knowledge Park, Tech Zone, Pari Chowk), the Yamuna Expressway and Jewar corridor under YEIDA, and the Gurugram-Manesar belt. Its project list includes Yotta’s Greater Noida campus, NTT in Sector 142, STT GDC in Sector 143, Sify in Sector 132 and AdaniConneX in Sectors 62 and 80. Yotta lists 30 MW of IT load at its D1 building in Greater Noida.

YEIDA lists a 100-acre Data Centre Park in Sector 28, the same sector as its Medical Devices Park. AdaniConneX lists 150 MW of potential capacity in Noida, and AM Green signed an MoU with Uttar Pradesh in January 2026 for a 1 GW AI data centre in the Greater Noida region, with first capacity targeted for 2028.

sections.heading: The UP Data Centre Policy 2026

blocks.text: Uttar Pradesh notified its Data Centre Policy 2026 by G.O. 536/78-2-2026 dated 9 July 2026, repealing the 2021 policy. Parks are 40 MW or more; units are above 2 MW and below 40 MW. Parks get an interest subsidy with an overall ceiling of Rs 50 crore and a dual-grid subsidy; units get a capital subsidy with a ceiling of Rs 20 crore. Booster incentives can raise both ceilings.

items: Land subsidy of 25% of prevailing sector rates on land from state agencies in Madhyanchal and Paschimanchal; Gautam Buddha Nagar is listed in Paschimanchal.
100% stamp duty exemption on purchase or lease from a government authority, against a bank guarantee released at commencement of commercial operation.

Base FAR 3.0 free plus 1.0 chargeable; basement parking, storage and DG set space sit outside FAR, rooftop chillers can be installed without counting in FAR, and ground coverage is up to 60% or as per byelaws.

Units get a 100% electricity duty exemption for 10 years. Wheeling and transmission charges on intrastate purchase are 50% exempt (75% for renewable power from within the state), and 100% exempt on the intrastate system for interstate purchase, for 25 years, until the first eight parks or 2 GW.
Data centres are classified as an essential service under ESMA, and the state agency assesses water availability before allotting land.

blocks.text: Gurugram and Manesar are in Haryana, so Uttar Pradesh’s terms do not apply there. Compare both states’ terms for an NCR search; the right answer depends on load size and the power route.

sections.heading: Power and water in NCR

blocks.text: Under the UP Supply Code, contracted loads above 10,000 kVA are supplied at 132 kV or 220 kV, and supply on an independent feeder depends on technical feasibility and bay or corridor availability at the substation. UPERC’s FY 2026-27 order prices HV-2 large and heavy power, which covers IT and ITeS units decided by the state through a policy notification, at Rs 6.10 per kVAh above 132 kV and Rs 6.40 above 66 kV up to 132 kV in urban areas, plus Rs 270 per kVA per month.

The UP policy reimburses the cost of one grid in a dual-grid connection for parks and cuts wheeling and transmission charges, which matters for green open access contracts. Ask for the specific substation and the DISCOM’s sanction letter; sector-level claims of available power do not tell you what is left for a new load.

Groundwater is a harder constraint. CGWA guidelines bar groundwater NOCs for new industries other than MSMEs in over-exploited assessment units, and SBI lists Gurugram among the water-stressed data centre metros. Plan for treated wastewater or air and closed-loop cooling.

sections.heading: Site risks in Noida and NCR

items: Seismic: Delhi is Zone IV (zone factor 0.24) in the IS 1893 (Part 1):2002 town list, a higher design load than Mumbai, Chennai or Hyderabad. Confirm the zone for the specific YEIDA sector.

Airport: Noida International Airport at Jewar began commercial operations on 15 June 2026. In July 2025 the airport advised that no construction or tree planting proceed within 20 km without a height clearance or NOC from AAI.

blocks.text: Invariant checks the evidence behind a site’s power (the DISCOM or transmission connection, the open access route, the nearest substations and what else is queued on them), screens seismic zone, flood history, groundwater status and airport height limits, and lists the central and state approvals the project needs with the authority behind each one. In NCR the groundwater unit and the Jewar height surface are checked alongside the power route.

title: Data centres in Bengaluru: capacity, Whitefield, Hoskote and water (2026)
description: Bengaluru had 162 MW of operational data centre capacity in H1 2026, mostly in Whitefield, with 28% vacancy. Karnataka’s 2026-31 policy plans parks at Hoskote, Mysuru and Mangaluru; water is the binding issue.
intro: Bengaluru is a mid-sized data centre market in a city Anarock describes as having a large concentration of IT firms, global capability centres and startups. Cushman & Wakefield counted 162 MW operational in H1 2026, about 9% of the top seven cities, with only 8 MW under construction and 28% colocation vacancy. Most capacity is in Whitefield in the east. Karnataka’s Sustainable Data Centre Policy 2026-31 targets 1 GW of IT load by 2031 and pays for low PUE and water efficiency. Water is the constraint: Newslaundry reports that most of the city’s data centres sit in its worst water-stressed areas.
takeaways: Bengaluru had 162 MW operational, 8 MW under construction and 92 MW planned in H1 2026 (Cushman & Wakefield). Anarock counts 137 MW IT.
Peripheral East (Whitefield) holds 128 MW; Peripheral South (Electronic City) 22 MW. Anarock names Devanahalli in the north as the primary hyperscale growth corridor.
Karnataka’s 2026-31 policy pays Rs 20 crore for PUE between 1.00 and 1.20 sustained for three years and plans parks at Hoskote, Mysuru and Mangaluru.
Newslaundry, citing the CGWB, reports that Bengaluru extracts almost 10 times the groundwater it recharges each year.

blocks.text: Cushman & Wakefield attributes the high colocation vacancy to relatively muted enterprise demand and low hyperscaler activity. Anarock forecasts 400 MW IT by 2030.

sections.heading: Sub-markets: Whitefield, Electronic City, Devanahalli and Hoskote

blocks.text: Whitefield and the eastern periphery hold most live capacity, 128 of 162 MW. Anarock lists NTT’s Bengaluru 4 in Electronic City, about 67 MW of IT load, among upcoming supply, and names Devanahalli and North Bengaluru as the primary hyperscale growth corridor.

Cushman & Wakefield reports a planned 500 MW data centre park near Hoskote, with the government committing solar power and treated water, and 500 MW planned at Mysuru and Mangaluru. The 2026-31 policy offers park land on 30 plus 30 year leases with dual-grid power connectivity.

sections.heading: Karnataka’s Sustainable Data Centre Policy 2026-31

items: A target of 1 GW of cumulative data centre IT load by 2031.
A one-time PUE incentive of Rs 20 crore for PUE between 1.00 and 1.20, paid in the fourth year after the PUE is shown for three consecutive years.
WUE reimbursement up to Rs 30 lakh a year for two years at 0.7 to 1.3 litres per kWh, and treated water reimbursement up to Rs 8 lakh a year for five years.
Customised packages for strategically important projects above Rs 3,000 crore, including cable landing stations and desalination plants.

blocks.text: Anarock notes the earlier Karnataka Data Centre Policy 2022-27. Check which policy a project falls under before relying on its terms.

sections.heading: Water: the binding constraint

blocks.text: Newslaundry reported in April 2026 that most of Bengaluru’s data centres are in the eastern and south-eastern tech corridors around Whitefield and Electronic City, running through the city’s worst water-stressed areas in summer, and quoted a hydrologist saying data centres mostly consume groundwater. Citing the CGWB, it reported that Bengaluru extracts almost 10 times the water it recharges each year.

Under CGWA guidelines, new industries other than MSMEs cannot get groundwater NOCs in over-exploited assessment units, and expansion that increases abstraction there is not allowed. Anarock estimates about 25.5 million litres per MW per year for cooling towers, so a new Bengaluru site needs a water plan, such as treated water or air-cooled or closed-loop systems, from day one.

sections.heading: Other site risks in Bengaluru

items: Seismic: Bengaluru is Zone II (zone factor 0.10) in the IS 1893 (Part 1):2002 town list.
Airport: Anarock cites airport connectivity as an advantage of Devanahalli and North Bengaluru. AAI height NOCs apply up to 20 km from VFR airports and 56 km from IFR airports.

title: Data centres in Pune: capacity, Hinjewadi, PBD North and power (2026)
description: Pune had 133 MW of operational data centre capacity in H1 2026 (Cushman & Wakefield), concentrated in the PBD North cluster and Hinjewadi, with a Microsoft Azure cloud region and Maharashtra’s data centre incentives.
intro: Cushman & Wakefield counted 133 MW of operational data centre capacity in Pune in H1 2026 across 12 facilities, about 7% of India’s operational capacity, with 31 MW under construction and 227 MW planned. Savills counts 182 MW IT, about 10% of the national total. Capacity is concentrated in the PBD North cluster and Hinjewadi. According to Cushman & Wakefield, Microsoft Azure has a cloud region in Pune and has acquired land for captive cloud developments, and Structure Research describes Pune as a core cloud region for one major hyperscaler because of its proximity to Mumbai. Maharashtra’s state data centre policies apply in Pune as in Mumbai.
takeaways: Pune had 133 MW operational, 31 MW under construction and 227 MW planned in H1 2026 (Cushman & Wakefield). Savills counts 182 MW IT.
PBD North holds 92 MW in 2 facilities at 16.5% vacancy; Hinjewadi 37 MW in 5, at 32.5% vacancy.
Maharashtra’s IT/ITES Policy 2023 and the Integrated Green Data Centre Parks framework, extended statewide in June 2026, apply in Pune.
Pune is Seismic Zone III in the IS 1893 (Part 1):2002 town list.

sections.heading: Power and policy in Pune

blocks.text: Maharashtra’s IT/ITES Policy 2023 gives a 100% stamp duty exemption on land or premises for a new data centre, and a Rs 1 per unit tariff subsidy for 5 years for new units outside Zone I; a notification of 22 June 2026 exempts data centre units from electricity duty for 20 years. A June 2026 government resolution extended the Integrated Green Data Centre Parks framework to the whole state, raised the number of eligible parks from 3 to 20, and cut the green power requirement for core operations from 100% to 51%.

The MERC Supply Code sets 33 kV supply up to 10,000 kVA of contract demand (20,000 kVA in a Metropolitan Area or on an express feeder elsewhere), extra high voltage above that, and a one-year standard where a new distribution substation is needed. MERC classifies data centres under the industrial category.

Structure Research reports that MSEDCL has allocated about 6 GW of grid power to data centres in Navi Mumbai and that committed and under-construction capacity there is approaching that level. Confirm the serving substation and sanction for the specific Pune plot.

Airport: AAI height clearance under GSR 751(E) applies within 20 km of the aerodrome reference point for visual flight rules airports, or 56 km for instrument flight rules airports.
Water: check the groundwater assessment unit and the municipal or MIDC supply before planning evaporative cooling.
