title: Data centres in Visakhapatnam: Google’s AI hub, gigawatt campuses and risks (2026)
description: Visakhapatnam has more than 4 GW of early-stage or announced data centre capacity, led by Google’s US$15 billion AI hub. The checks are power relative to the city’s demand, cyclone exposure, water and new cable landings.
intro: Invest India and Cushman & Wakefield map more than 4 GW of early-stage or announced data centre capacity in Visakhapatnam. Google committed about US$15 billion over 2026 to 2030 for its first India AI hub here, with AdaniConneX and Nxtra by Airtel, and broke ground at Tarluvada on 28 April 2026. Digital Connexion (1 GW), Colt DCS with RMZ (1.25 GW) and AirTrunk (up to 1.8 GW across two proposed campuses) have announced or proposed large developments. Crisil estimates that by FY2030 data centre capacity in Visakhapatnam could equal about 80% of the city’s current peak power demand.
takeaways: Announced: Google (about US$15 billion, about 1 GW), Digital Connexion (about US$11 billion, 1 GW), Colt DCS and RMZ (1.25 GW, about US$21 billion), AirTrunk (up to 1.8 GW in Anakapalli, proposed).
Andhra Pradesh Data Center Policy 4.0 (2024-29) gives large projects project-specific packages through government orders; the state issued orders for specific projects in 2026.
Cyclone Hudhud crossed the coast over Visakhapatnam on 12 October 2014 with winds of about 180 km/h and a 1.4 m storm surge.
New subsea routes: Google’s America-India Connect gateway and Sify’s open cable landing station.

Andhra Pradesh grants incentives for large projects project by project through government orders. Read the project order; the policy text alone does not tell you what a given site gets.

sections.heading: Disadvantages and risks of a data centre in Vizag

items: Cyclone: Hudhud crossed the coast over Visakhapatnam on 12 October 2014 with maximum sustained winds of about 180 km/h, central pressure of 950 hPa and a 1.4 m storm surge at the Visakhapatnam tide gauge. Design for wind loads and plan for grid outages after landfall.
Water: check the groundwater category of the assessment unit before planning evaporative cooling; nationally, 10.8% of assessment units were over-exploited in the 2025 assessment.
Market depth: Invest India and Cushman & Wakefield map Visakhapatnam’s capacity as early-stage or announced, so early tenants depend on the hyperscale anchors.
Seismic: Visakhapatnam is Zone II (zone factor 0.10), a low design load.

In Vizag the questions are which transmission scheme and substation serve the plot, the cyclone design basis, and the water source.

sections.heading: Cable landings on the east coast

blocks.text: Google’s America-India Connect, announced on 18 February 2026, includes a new international subsea gateway in Visakhapatnam, a direct path from Vizag and Chennai to South Africa, and a direct path between Vizag and Singapore. At the Google groundbreaking, Airtel cited a next-generation cable landing station as part of what it brings to the Vizag hub, and Sify is building an open cable landing station alongside its 50 MW AI edge data centre.

title: Data centres in Gujarat: Jamnagar, GIFT City, Ahmedabad and Dholera (2026)
description: Gujarat’s data centre projects include Reliance’s AI campus at Jamnagar, Yotta’s GIFT City facility and a planned 250 MW campus at Dholera. The 2026-29 state policy supports projects of 150 MW or more.
intro: Gujarat’s data centre activity centres on a few large projects. Mukesh Ambani said in February 2026 that Reliance had begun building multi-gigawatt data centres at Jamnagar, with more than 120 MW expected online in the second half of 2026; Meta agreed in June 2026 to lease capacity at a 168 MW Reliance facility there. GIFT City hosts Yotta’s 1 MW G1 facility, and L&T Vyoma signed an MoU for a 250 MW green data centre at Dholera. The Viksit Gujarat Data Centre Policy 2026-29, launched on 9 July 2026, supports only projects of 150 MW or more, with incentives available until 7.5 GW of capacity is reached statewide.
takeaways: Jamnagar: Reliance AI campus; Meta leasing capacity at a 168 MW facility (June 2026); Google and Reliance dedicated AI cloud region announced (August 2025). Invest India and Cushman & Wakefield map Jamnagar at 1 GW+ early stage; Anarock lists a 3 GW campus.

Gujarat’s 2026-29 policy requires at least 150 MW of approved IT load and 51% green power for core operations, and, according to Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas, treats data centre operations as an essential service under the Gujarat ESMA 1972.
GIFT City: Yotta G1, 350 racks and 1 MW IT load. The Union Budget 2023-24 announced that the government would facilitate data embassies in GIFT IFSC.
Dholera: L&T Vyoma MoU for a 250 MW green data centre, Rs 25,000 crore, with operations expected by 2028.

sections.heading: Jamnagar: Reliance’s AI campus

blocks.text: Reliance announced a Rs 10 trillion (about US$110 billion) plan to build AI computing infrastructure over seven years on 19 February 2026, and said construction of multi-gigawatt data centres at Jamnagar had begun, with more than 120 MW expected online in the second half of 2026, supported by 10 GW of surplus solar power in Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh. Reliance and Google announced a dedicated AI cloud region, starting with a data centre in Jamnagar, in August 2025.

Meta announced its first Indian AI data centre partnership with Reliance on 10 June 2026: Meta is leasing capacity at a 168 MW facility at Jamnagar that Reliance said will be ready within two years, powered by renewable energy and cooled with desalinated seawater.

sections.heading: GIFT City, Ahmedabad and Dholera

blocks.text: GIFT City, India’s first international financial services centre, at Gandhinagar, hosts Yotta’s G1 facility with 1 MW of IT load. In the Union Budget 2023-24 the Finance Minister said the government would facilitate data embassies in GIFT IFSC for countries looking for digital continuity solutions.

At the India AI Impact Summit in February 2026, Gujarat signed an MoU with L&T Vyoma for a 250 MW green data centre at the Dholera Special Investment Region, with Rs 25,000 crore of investment and operations expected by 2028. The state policy document highlights Dholera and GIFT City among Gujarat’s industrial hubs.

sections.heading: The Viksit Gujarat Data Centre Policy 2026-29

items: Eligible projects need at least 150 MW of approved installed IT load, and at least 51% of electricity for core operations must come from green and renewable energy.
Power tariff subsidy of Rs 1 per unit for 20 years; 100% electricity duty reimbursement for 20 years; 100% stamp duty and registration fee exemption on lease or purchase of land.

Interest subsidy up to 4% a year for 10 years (capped at Rs 25 crore a year); capital subsidy of 2.5% of eligible fixed capital investment for projects solely in Dholera SIR; total incentives capped at 75% of eligible fixed capital investment.

Open access permitted and dual power supply through two independent feeders; data centre operations treated as an essential service under the Gujarat Essential Services Maintenance Act, 1972, according to Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas.
Operative for three years from notification (extendable), with incentives available only until 7.5 GW of installed capacity is reached statewide.

blocks.text: Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas describes the policy as designed for hyperscale and large data centre developments, in contrast to the previous framework for smaller projects.

sections.heading: Site risks in Gujarat

items: Seismic: Ahmedabad is Zone III (zone factor 0.16) in the IS 1893 (Part 1):2002 town list, while Bhuj in Kutch is Zone V (zone factor 0.36). Check the zone for the specific site.
Water: Reliance’s 168 MW Jamnagar facility for Meta will be cooled with desalinated seawater, and the state policy offers a capital subsidy for captive desalination plants.

blocks.text: Invariant checks the evidence behind a site’s power (the DISCOM or transmission connection, the open access route, the nearest substations and what else is queued on them), screens seismic zone, flood history, groundwater status and airport height limits, and lists the central and state approvals the project needs with the authority behind each one. In Gujarat, we check the 150 MW policy floor and the water source alongside the power route.

title: Data centres in Kolkata and East India: New Town, Salt Lake and Bhubaneswar (2026)
description: Kolkata had 22 MW of operational data centre capacity in H1 2026, mostly in New Town. West Bengal’s 2021 policy classed data centres as essential services; its five-year term ran to September 2026.
intro: Kolkata is the smallest of the seven city markets in Cushman & Wakefield’s H1 2026 count: 22 MW operational across six facilities, 18 MW in New Town and 4 MW in Salt Lake, with 13 MW under construction and 71 MW planned. Cushman & Wakefield attributes demand mainly to government and small and medium enterprises. West Bengal’s Data Centre Policy 2021 classed data centre organisations as essential services and treated their electricity as industrial; it was valid for five years from September 2021, and in May 2026 the state BJP president said the new government was formulating a new data centre policy. Odisha’s 2022 policy is another incentive regime in the region.
takeaways: Kolkata had 22 MW operational, 13 MW under construction and 71 MW planned in H1 2026, with 19.4% colocation vacancy (Cushman & Wakefield).
New Town holds 18 MW and Salt Lake 4 MW. Cushman & Wakefield reports a cable landing station under construction at Tajpur.
West Bengal Data Centre Policy 2021 (notified 6 September 2021): essential services classification, 100% stamp duty exemption, 5-year electricity duty waiver, FAR 3.0 plus 1.0 purchasable.
The government named West Bengal, with Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh, among states coming up as new data centre investment destinations.

W.Media reported in February 2025 that NTT Global Data Centers had inaugurated its Kolkata data centre. In August 2026 the government told the Rajya Sabha that the data centre industry is expanding in states including West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh.

items: Notification No. 490-Estt/ITE-18011/2/2021 dated 6 September 2021, operative for five years or until replaced.

Yotta lists Bhubaneswar among its planned edge data centre cities.

Flood: check drainage and plot elevation on low-lying land.
Airport: AAI height clearance applies within 20 km of the aerodrome reference point for visual flight rules airports, or 56 km for instrument flight rules airports.

title: Data centre companies in India: the largest operators and recent deals (2026)
description: The largest data centre companies in India by market share are NTT, Sify, STT GDC, Nxtra and CtrlS (Anarock, H1 2026), with Yotta, AdaniConneX and new entrants such as AirTrunk, TCS HyperVault and CoreWeave.
intro: Five operators lead Anarock’s H1 2026 market share table for India: it puts NTT at 21%, Sify and STT GDC at 19% each, and Nxtra (Airtel) and CtrlS at 15% each, followed by Yotta at 5%. Other operators include AdaniConneX, Princeton Digital, Iron Mountain, Equinix, Digital Edge and CapitaLand, and hyperscalers build their own campuses. Deals in 2026 included a US$1 billion investment in Nxtra, up to Rs 7,000 crore from CPP Investments for CtrlS, AirTrunk’s acquisition of Lumina CloudInfra, and a planned 240 MW CoreWeave deployment at AdaniConneX.
takeaways: Anarock H1 2026 shares: NTT 21%, Sify 19%, STT GDC 19%, Nxtra 15%, CtrlS 15%, Yotta 5%, Princeton Digital 3%, Iron Mountain (Web Werks) 2%, AdaniConneX 1%. Anarock does not state the base.
Company-stated capacity is not comparable across operators: some report built IT load, some operational capacity, some potential capacity.
Hyperscalers (AWS, Microsoft, Google) build their own campuses and are not in Anarock’s share table.
New entrants since 2025: AirTrunk (through Lumina CloudInfra), TCS HyperVault, and CoreWeave as a tenant.

sections.heading: New entrants and global operators

items: Equinix opened MB3, its fourth Mumbai data centre, in April 2026 with an initial investment of over US$95 million, taking its cumulative investment in India to over US$365 million.
Digital Edge is developing a planned 400 MW campus in Navi Mumbai; BOM2 topped out and BOM3 construction began in August 2026, which with BOM1 brings the campus to close to 120 MW.
CapitaLand is building a facility with 53 MW of gross power capacity in Ambattur, Chennai, due by the end of 2026.
AirTrunk, backed by Blackstone and CPPIB, acquired Lumina CloudInfra in April 2026, gaining about 600 MW of planned capacity; Lumina operates in Mumbai, Chennai and Hyderabad.
Colt DCS and RMZ formed a 50:50 joint venture to invest US$1.7 billion in November 2024, starting with existing sites in Navi Mumbai and Ambattur, Chennai.
TCS HyperVault, with up to Rs 18,000 crore committed by TCS and TPG, aims for capacity above 1 GW; OpenAI is its first customer, starting with 100 MW.
Digital Connexion, the Reliance, Brookfield and Digital Realty joint venture, launched a Chennai campus built for up to 100 MW of IT load in January 2024 and plans 1 GW in Visakhapatnam.

sections.heading: Hyperscalers building their own data centres

blocks.text: AWS, Microsoft and Google run or are building their own campuses. AWS operates regions in Mumbai and Hyderabad, Microsoft runs four Indian regions including India South Central in Hyderabad, and Google is building its AI hub in Visakhapatnam with AdaniConneX and Airtel. Invest India and Cushman & Wakefield report that hyperscalers took more than 80% of absorption in H1 2026.

For a buyer of capacity, the useful question is not which company is largest but which one has firm power for the MW and date you need. Ask for the DISCOM sanction or connection agreement behind the hall you would occupy.

title: Mumbai vs Chennai vs Hyderabad for data centres: power, policy and risk (2026)
description: Mumbai has scale and cables but a nearly committed grid allocation; Chennai has cables and high vacancy but flood risk; Hyderabad has the second-largest pipeline and the lowest seismic zone of the three.
intro: Mumbai, Chennai and Hyderabad are India’s three main choices for a large data centre, and each wins on a different test. Mumbai has about half of top-seven-city live capacity (Cushman & Wakefield), 13 cable landing stations and the lowest vacancy of the three, but Structure Research reports that committed capacity is approaching its Navi Mumbai grid allocation. Chennai has seven landing stations and 26.7% colocation vacancy, but carries flood risk, and its 2021 state policy covers data centres incorporated by 31 March 2026. Hyderabad has the second largest pipeline, Microsoft and AWS regions and Seismic Zone II, but as an inland city no cable landings.
takeaways: Pick Mumbai for interconnection and latency to cables; plan for power evidence to be the hardest part.
Pick Chennai for available halls today and east-coast cables; check flood exposure at plot level.
Pick Hyderabad for a large pipeline and, on Crisil’s ratio, more power headroom relative to city demand; accept no local cable landing.
Rents are within a narrow band across the three; land and power date differ far more.

sections.heading: Which city fits which project

items: Interconnection, cloud on-ramps and financial services: Mumbai, where Cushman & Wakefield’s main clusters are Thane-Belapur Road and Powai.

A 100 MW+ hyperscale or AI campus: South Hyderabad (634 MW planned), Mumbai’s outer belt (Panvel, Taloja) if a substation date is firm, or Visakhapatnam.
Lowest seismic zone of the three: Hyderabad (Zone II).

faqs.question: Is Mumbai or Chennai better for a data centre?

faqs.question: Why is Hyderabad growing as a data center market?

title: India vs Singapore vs Johor for data centres: power, policy and cost (2026)
description: Singapore releases capacity through allocation calls, Malaysia’s TNB has signed GW-scale data centre supply deals, and India offers lower build cost, rents 30 to 35% below peers and a tax holiday to 2047.
intro: India, Singapore and Johor in Malaysia are alternative locations for Asian cloud and AI capacity, under very different constraints. Singapore had about 1.4 GW across more than 70 data centres in 2024 and now releases new capacity through allocation calls; its second call in December 2025 offered at least 200 MW with a PUE of 1.25 at full load. Malaysia’s utility TNB had signed electricity supply agreements for 59 data centre projects totalling 8.3 GW by July 2026, while Johor introduced a higher water tariff for data centres in August 2025. India had roughly 1.8 GW live in H1 2026, build costs that Cushman & Wakefield puts about 23% below Malaysia, and a tax holiday to 2047 for foreign cloud companies using Indian data centres.
takeaways: Singapore: capacity is allocated, not open. DC-CFA2 (launched 1 December 2025) offered at least 200 MW with PUE 1.25 at full load, Green Mark Platinum and at least 50% green energy pathways.

Malaysia: TNB had 59 data centre projects and 8.3 GW under electricity supply agreements by July 2026 (RHB Research). Johor has a state technical committee that evaluates data centre projects for water impact, and set a data centre water tariff from 1 August 2025.
India: build cost about US$7.4 million per MW (Cushman & Wakefield), rents 30 to 35% below peer markets (Crisil), and 11 states with dedicated data centre policies.
The figures are not like for like: Singapore’s is a 2024 capacity figure published by EDB, Malaysia’s is capacity under TNB supply agreements, India’s is operational capacity from market reports.

sections.heading: Singapore: scarce capacity, strict conditions

blocks.text: Singapore imposed a moratorium on new data centres in 2019 and relaxed it through a pilot call for applications launched in July 2022, under which operators secured 80 MW in 2023. Its Green Data Centre Roadmap, launched on 30 May 2024, set out at least 300 MW of additional capacity in the next few years and another 200 MW for operators using green energy. The second Data Centre Call for Application opened on 1 December 2025 for at least 200 MW and its application window closed on 31 March 2026.

Selected applicants must reach PUE of 1.25 or better at full design load, obtain Green Mark for Data Centres 2024 Platinum, and power at least half of the new capacity through eligible green pathways such as biomethane, low-carbon hydrogen or ammonia, or building-integrated solar. Morgan Lewis notes that land scarcity and strict controls have led global tech firms to look to alternatives such as Johor.

sections.heading: Malaysia and Johor: power agreements and water

blocks.text: RHB Research, reported by The Star in July 2026, counted TNB electricity supply agreements for 59 data centre projects with a combined 8.3 GW, of which 36 projects with a maximum capacity of 4.5 GW were completed. These are Malaysia-wide figures under supply agreements, not a measure of IT load in use.

Water is a stated concern in Johor. In August 2025 the state said it was the only state with a technical committee dedicated to evaluating and approving data centre projects, particularly their impact on water resources, amid concerns about a possible treated water shortfall by 2030. A data centre water tariff of RM5.33 per cubic metre took effect on 1 August 2025.

sections.heading: India: lower cost, state-by-state rules

blocks.text: India’s advantages are cost and scale. Cushman & Wakefield puts construction at about US$7.4 million per MW, about 23% below Malaysia and 26% below Australia, and Crisil reports Indian rents 30 to 35% below peer markets. The Budget 2026-27 tax holiday to 2047 applies to foreign companies serving global customers using data centre services in India.

The trade-offs include grid allocation and state-by-state rules. There is no notified national data centre policy, and states set their own incentives. Structure Research reports that committed capacity is approaching MSEDCL’s data centre grid allocation in Navi Mumbai, pushing new Mumbai builds to Panvel, Taloja and Rasayani. Beyond Mumbai, Hyderabad holds 18% of upcoming supply and Cushman & Wakefield maps more than 4 GW of early-stage or announced capacity at Visakhapatnam.

faqs.question: Is India cheaper than Singapore for data centres?
faqs.answer: India’s costs are low against regional peers: Cushman & Wakefield puts construction at about US$7.4 million per MW, about 23% below Malaysia, and Crisil reports Indian rents 30 to 35% below peer markets. New Singapore capacity is released through allocation calls with strict efficiency and green power conditions.

faqs.question: How much data centre capacity does Singapore have?
faqs.answer: About 1.4 GW across more than 70 data centres, per the Singapore Economic Development Board in May 2024, with at least 300 MW more planned in the next few years.

faqs.question: What water rules apply to data centres in Johor?
faqs.answer: Johor has a state technical committee that evaluates and approves data centre projects, particularly their impact on water resources, and has charged data centres a water tariff of RM5.33 per cubic metre since 1 August 2025.

faqs.question: What is Singapore’s DC-CFA2?
faqs.answer: The second Data Centre Call for Application, launched 1 December 2025, allocating at least 200 MW to applicants meeting PUE 1.25 at full load, Green Mark for Data Centres 2024 Platinum and at least 50% green energy pathways.

faqs.question: Does India have a data center tax incentive for foreign cloud companies?
faqs.answer: Yes. Budget 2026-27 introduced a tax holiday from tax year 2026-27 to 2046-47 for foreign companies providing cloud services globally using data centre services from India, with sales to Indian users through an Indian reseller.

title: AI data centres in India: gigawatt campuses, IndiaAI GPUs and power (2026)
description: India’s AI data centre build-out includes gigawatt-scale campuses in Visakhapatnam and Jamnagar, while IndiaAI Mission compute passed 38,000 GPUs at Rs 65 per hour in February 2026 and 45,000 by June 2026.
intro: AI demand is bringing gigawatt-scale campuses to India’s data centre market. Google broke ground on a gigawatt-scale AI hub in Visakhapatnam in April 2026, Reliance has begun building multi-gigawatt data centres at Jamnagar and is to build a 168 MW AI-ready data centre to be leased by Meta, OpenAI is TCS HyperVault’s first customer with 100 MW and plans to scale to 1 GW, and CoreWeave plans 240 MW at AdaniConneX in Navi Mumbai. The government’s IndiaAI Mission had more than 38,000 GPUs onboarded at Rs 65 per hour by February 2026 and more than 45,000 in its shared compute capacity by June 2026. Invest India and Cushman & Wakefield’s AI scenario puts India at about 8 GW by 2030.
takeaways: Announced gigawatt-scale AI campuses: Google in Visakhapatnam, Reliance at Jamnagar, Digital Connexion in Visakhapatnam, TCS HyperVault, AM Green in Greater Noida (MoU).
IndiaAI GPU pool: 18,693 (January 2025), 34,333 (May 2025), 38,000+ at Rs 65 per hour (February 2026), 45,000+ (June 2026).
Anarock puts an Nvidia H100 GPU cluster at 30 to 60 kW per rack against 8 to 10 kW traditionally. Power per GPU, not floor area, sizes the site.

sections.heading: Power for AI data centres in India

blocks.text: An AI campus is sized by power per GPU. Anarock puts an Nvidia H100 GPU cluster at 30 to 60 kW per rack against 8 to 10 kW traditionally, and SBI notes that air cooling approaches its limits beyond about 15 kW per rack, leading to early adoption of direct-to-chip and immersion cooling. A 100 MW AI hall therefore needs a high-voltage grid connection with a firm energisation date.

Crisil estimates Visakhapatnam’s data centre capacity could equal about 80% of the city’s current peak demand by FY2030. Reliance says its build-out will be supported by its green energy capacity, including surplus solar power in Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh.

title: Data centre investment in India: hyperscaler commitments and deals (2026)
description: Invest India and Cushman & Wakefield count announced data centre investment in India above US$180 billion by September 2026, including Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Reliance and Adani. Check the power behind each campus.
intro: Invest India and Cushman & Wakefield count disclosed data centre investment commitments in India of US$27 billion in 2023, US$29.6 billion in 2024, US$56.4 billion in 2025 and US$184 billion in January to September 2026. Amazon has committed US$48 billion for 2026 to 2030, Microsoft US$17.5 billion for 2026 to 2029, and Google about US$15 billion for its Visakhapatnam AI hub. Reliance announced a plan of about US$110 billion for AI computing infrastructure, and Cushman & Wakefield reports an Adani commitment of US$100 billion through 2035 for AI-ready data centres and associated infrastructure. The Budget 2026-27 added a tax holiday to 2047 for foreign cloud companies using Indian data centres.
takeaways: Disclosed commitments: US$184 billion in January to September 2026 alone (Invest India and Cushman & Wakefield). CBRE counts Rs 15.29 lakh crore (US$173 billion) cumulative since 2021.
Equity mix of current investments: about 61% foreign, 39% domestic (Invest India and Cushman & Wakefield).
Long-tenor debt costs about 9.5 to 10.5% for up to 12 years, helped by infrastructure status (Anarock).
A commitment is not capacity. The diligence question is whether the campus has a firm power connection and date.

sections.heading: How much has been committed, and why the totals differ

blocks.text: Invest India and Cushman & Wakefield count announced investment above US$180 billion as of September 2026, with US$184 billion disclosed in January to September 2026 alone and an equity mix of about 61% foreign and 39% domestic. CBRE, as reported by IBEF, counts Rs 3.34 lakh crore (US$38 billion) in H1 2026 and Rs 15.29 lakh crore (US$173 billion) since 2021. Anarock cites more than US$300 billion of commitments.

The totals are not comparable: they can mix multi-year plans, group-wide AI programmes that include more than data centres, and MoUs that may not proceed. For underwriting, count only projects with land, a power connection agreement and a construction start.

sections.heading: What to diligence before investing in an Indian data centre

items: Power: the DISCOM sanction letter or transmission connection agreement, the substation and voltage, the energisation date, and what else is queued on the same substation.

Policy: which state policy applies, whether its window is still open (Tamil Nadu’s 2021 policy covers data centres incorporated by 31 March 2026), and whether incentives are in a project-specific order.
Site: seismic zone, flood history, groundwater unit status, airport height limits and coastal rules.
Contracts: tenor (Crisil reports tenors have lengthened to 15 to 20 years), tenant concentration and power pass-through.

blocks.text: Data centres of 5 MW or more of IT load were added to the infrastructure list on 11 October 2022. Anarock says infrastructure status has improved access to long-tenor financing, at about 9.5 to 10.5% for tenors of up to 12 years.
